div.p: The confidence of Christians is the resurrection of the dead; in believing it we are what we are. Truth compels us to believe it, and God lays open the truth; but the crowd mocks, supposing that nothing remains after death. And yet they offer sacrifices to the dead, and that with the most lavish observance, providing for their tastes and for the seasons of their feasting — so that those whom they deny to have any feeling, they presume nevertheless still to have desires. But I shall mock the crowd the more, precisely when it burns the dead most cruelly and then most greedily feeds them, in the same fires both serving and offending them. What piety, that makes sport of cruelty! Does it sacrifice or insult, when it cremates the cremated? Plainly, even the wise men sometimes join their verdict to the crowd's. That nothing exists after death is the school of Epicurus. Seneca too says that all things end after death, even death itself.

Yet it is enough that the philosophy of Pythagoras and Empedocles and the Platonists, no smaller, cries out to the contrary that the soul is immortal — indeed they go further and most nearly affirm that it may return into bodies, though not into the same ones, though not into human bodies only, so that Euphorbus is reckoned to pass into Pythagoras, and Homer into a peacock. Certainly they pronounced the soul's return to be bodily, having altered its quality more tolerably than they would have done by denying it — at least knocking at the truth, though not entering it. So the present age is not ignorant of the resurrection of the dead, even when it errs.

But if even in God's sight there is some sect more akin to the Epicureans than to the prophets, we shall know what the Sadducees are to hear from Christ. For it was reserved to Christ to lay bare all things hidden from of old, to set right what was doubtful, to make full what had only been foretasted, to make present what had been proclaimed — and certainly the resurrection of the dead, which He proved not only through Himself but also in Himself. But now we are arrayed against other Sadducees, sharers in their opinion. For so they acknowledge half a resurrection — that of the soul alone — while they spurn the flesh, just as they spurn the very Lord of the flesh. In short, no others begrudge salvation to the bodily substance except the heretics of another divinity. And therefore, compelled to dispose of Christ in another way lest He be reckoned the Creator's, they first went astray about His very flesh, contending either that it is no true flesh at all (as Marcion and Basilides hold) or that it is of a peculiar quality (as the heresies of Valentinus and Apelles hold). And so it follows that they exclude salvation from that substance of which they deny Christ to be a partaker — certain that it is furnished with the supreme guarantee of the resurrection, if the flesh has already risen in Christ. For this reason we sent ahead the volume On the Flesh of Christ, in which we prove both that it is solid, against the emptiness of a phantasm, and that it is human, against any peculiarity of quality — its very condition having inscribed Christ as both man and Son of Man. For by proving Him fleshly and corporeal we likewise block our adversaries' way, laying down the rule that no other God is to be believed than the Creator, since we show such a Christ as the one in whom is recognized the God promised by the Creator. Being thus blocked concerning God the author of the flesh and Christ the redeemer of the flesh, they will now be refuted concerning the resurrection of the flesh as well. Fittingly, of course. And it is in roughly this manner that we say a dispute with the heretics ought to be entered upon. For the order of things always demands that one proceed from first principles, so that it may first be established who is said to have ordained the matter in question. And indeed the heretics, conscious of their weakness, never treat things in order. For knowing how hard they labour to insinuate another divinity against the God of the world — naturally known to all from the testimony of His works, and certainly prior in the sacraments and more manifest in the preachings — under the pretext of a more pressing cause, namely the seeking of human salvation itself before all else, they begin from questions about the resurrection, because the resurrection of the flesh is believed with more difficulty than the single divinity. And so, with their treatment stripped of the strength of its own order and burdened rather with scruples that disparage the flesh, little by little they bend men toward the sense of another divinity by the very shaking and alteration of their hope. For each man, cast down or moved from the standing of the hope he had received in the Creator, is easily turned aside to suspecting, even of his own accord, an author of another hope. For through diversity of promises a diversity of gods is insinuated. Thus we see many ensnared, undone about the resurrection of the flesh before they are undone about the unity of the divinity. Therefore, as regards the heretics, we have shown with what wedge they must be met by us. And it has been met already, each under its own title: concerning the one God and His Christ, against Marcion; concerning the flesh of the Lord, against four heresies, chiefly to lay the foundation for this present question — so that now the resurrection of the flesh alone may be treated as something held uncertain even among us, that is, with the Creator. For there are many untaught, and very many doubtful in their faith, and more who are simple, who will need to be instructed, directed, and fortified — because in this corner too the unity of the divinity is defended. For just as it is shaken when the resurrection of the flesh is denied, so it is made firm when the flesh is vindicated. The salvation of the soul, however, I believe needs no re-examination. For nearly all heretics, in whatever way, allow it; they do not, at any rate, deny it. Let some one Lucanus see to it — he who does not spare even this substance, but, dissolving it after Aristotle's manner, substitutes for it something else, intending to raise up some third thing, neither soul nor flesh, that is, not a man, but perhaps a bear, in so far as he is a Lucanus. He too has from us a most full treatise on the whole state of the soul, which we maintain to be above all immortal, while of the flesh alone we acknowledge both the failing and most especially assert the restoring — having reduced to the ordinary body of the material those matters which elsewhere too we have touched in passing and deferred, as the run of the argument required. For just as it is customary to give certain things a foretaste, so it is necessary to defer others — provided that what was foretasted is supplied in its own place and what was deferred is rendered under its own name.

There is indeed even a knowing of God's matters by the common senses; but for the testimony of the true, not for the support of the false — namely such as agrees with the divine, not against the divine, disposition. For some things are known even by nature: as the immortality of the soul, to many; as our God, to all. I will therefore use even the verdict of some Plato pronouncing, "Every soul is immortal"; I will use too the conscience of the people attesting "the God of gods." I will use also the other common senses, which proclaim God a judge: "God sees," and "I commend it to God." But when they say, "What is dead is dead," and "Live while you live," and "After death all things end, even death itself" — then I shall remember both that the heart of the crowd is accounted ash by God, and that the very wisdom of the world is pronounced foolishness. Then, if even the heretic takes refuge in the vices of the crowd or the dispositions of the world, I shall say: "Depart from the heathen, heretic. Although you are all one who feign a god, yet while you do this in the name of Christ, while you seem to yourself a Christian, you are other than the heathen: give him back his own perceptions, since he is not instructed by yours. Why do you lean on a blind guide, if you see? Why are you clothed by a naked man, if you have put on Christ? Why do you use another's shield, if you are armed by the apostle? Let him rather learn from you to confess the resurrection of the flesh than you from him to deny it; for if it were right that it should be denied even by Christians, it would be enough for them to be instructed out of their own knowledge, not out of the crowd's ignorance." So far is he from being a Christian who shall deny what Christians confess, and shall deny it by those arguments which a non-Christian uses. Take away from the heretics, in short, the things in which they think with the heathen, so that they rest their questions on the Scriptures alone, and they will not be able to stand. For it is simplicity itself, and the fellow-feeling of opinions, and the familiarity of views, that commends the common senses; and on that account they are thought the more trustworthy, because they define things that are bare and open and known to all. But the divine reason lies in the marrow, not on the surface, and is often at odds with what is manifest.

And so the heretics begin at once from there, and build their first foundation there, and afterwards build in between — from that point at which they know minds are easily caught, the agreeable fellowship of the senses. Would you hear anything sooner or more often from a heretic than from a heathen? And is it not at once and everywhere abuse of the flesh — abuse of its origin, its matter, its mischance, its whole end: unclean from the very beginning out of the dregs of the earth, more unclean thereafter out of the slime of its own seed; trifling, weak, criminal, burdensome, troublesome; and after this whole eulogy of ignominy, falling away into its origin, the earth, and into the name of "corpse," and from this name too perishing into no name at all thereafter, into the death of every term whatsoever? This, then, the flesh snatched from your sight and touch and memory — would you, a wise man, persuade us that it will one day receive itself back entire from corruption, solid from collapse, full from emptiness, into something at all out of nothing — and that too with fires and waves and the bellies of beasts and the crops of birds and the entrails of fishes giving it back, and with the very seasons' own appetite? And will the same flesh be hoped for that perished, so that the lame, the one-eyed, the blind, the leper, the paralytic return — and so that there is no pleasure in having gone back to one's former state? Or will they be whole, so that they fear to suffer such things again? What then of the consequences of the flesh? Will all things again be necessary to it, and first of all food and drink — must the lungs swim, the intestines seethe, the privy parts not be ashamed, all the members toil? Again ulcers and wounds and fever and gout and death to be wished for back? Doubtless these will be the prayers of the flesh recovered — to long once more to escape from it. And we indeed say these things somewhat more decently, out of respect for the pen. For the rest, you may find by experience in conversation with them — heathen and heretics alike — how far their foul speech may go.

Therefore, since the untaught still think from the common senses, and the doubtful and the simple are again disquieted through those same senses, and since everywhere this is the first ram aimed against us, by which the condition of the flesh is battered — necessarily the condition of the flesh must first be fortified by us, its disparagement driven off by praise. So the heretics provoke us to play the rhetorician as well as the philosopher. This useless and trifling little body, which they do not even shrink from calling an evil — though it had been the work of angels (as Menander and Marcus would have it), though it were the construction of some fiery angel as well (as Apelles teaches) — would suffice, by the patronage of a second divinity, to establish the authority of the flesh. We know angels to be after God. Now then, whoever that supreme god of any given heretic may be, I should not unreasonably derive the dignity of the flesh from him too, since from him would have come the will to produce it. For surely he would have forbidden to be made what he knew would be made, had he not willed it to be made. So even according to them the flesh is equally a thing of God. There is no work that is not his who allowed it to be. But it is well that even the more numerous and harsher doctrines yield the whole moulding of man to our God. How great this God is you know well enough, you who have believed Him to be the only one. Now let the flesh begin to please you, whose craftsman is so great. "But the world too," you say, "is God's work, and yet the fashion of this world passes away — the apostle himself being witness; nor will the restoration of the world be prejudged because it is God's work. And surely, if the whole is beyond reform after its passing, what of the part?" Plainly so — if the part is matched to the whole. But it is to a difference that we appeal. First, indeed, because all things were made by the word of God, and without it nothing was made. But the flesh was established by the word of God too, for the sake of its form, that nothing be without the word; for "Let us make man," He first sent forth, and further, "with His hand," for the sake of its precedence, that it might not be compared to the universe. "And God formed man," He says. The reason for so great a difference is, without doubt, in keeping with the condition of things. For the things that were being made were lesser than the one for whom they were made, since they were made for man, to whom soon after they were assigned by God. Rightly, then, did all things come forth like a handmaid, at His bidding and command and by the bare power of His voice. But man, as their lord, was for this reason fashioned by God Himself, that he might be able to be lord, by being made by the Lord. And remember that "man" is properly said of the flesh, which first laid claim to the name of man: "And God formed man, the slime of the earth." Now there is man, who as yet is slime. "And He breathed into his face the breath of life, and man" — that is, the slime — "became a living soul; and God placed the man whom He had formed in paradise." So far is man first the thing moulded, then the whole. This I have urged for this reason: that whatever has been provided and promised by God for man at all, you may know to be owed not to the soul alone but to the flesh as well — if not from a partnership of kind, certainly at least from the privilege of the name.

I will therefore pursue my purpose, if only I am able to claim for the flesh as much as He bestowed who made it — even then glorying that that little thing, slime, came into the hands of God, whatever those hands are, blessed enough though only by their touch. For what if, with no further work, the thing moulded had stood firm at once from the touch of God? So great was the matter in hand, by which this material was being built up. And so it is honoured as often as the hand of God handles it — while it is touched, while it is plucked, while it is drawn out, while it is shaped. Reckon up to it the whole God, occupied and devoted: with hand, sense, work, counsel, wisdom, providence, and above all with that very affection which was dictating the lineaments. For whatever was being expressed in the slime, Christ was in mind, the man who was to be — for the word too was both slime and flesh, since the earth too was such then. For so runs the Father's preface to the Son: "Let us make man after our image and likeness." And God made man — that, namely, which He had formed — after the image of God He made him; that is, of Christ. For the Word too is God, who, being established in the figure of God, thought it no robbery to be equal with God. So that slime, even then putting on the image of the Christ who was to come in the flesh, was not only God's work but also His pledge. To what end now does it serve, for the darkening of the flesh's origin, to bandy about the name of "earth," as of a sordid, low-lying element? — when, even if other matter had been fit for the fashioning of man, the eminence of the craftsman ought to be reconsidered, who both judged that matter worthy by choosing it and made it by handling it. The hands of Phidias work the Olympian Jupiter out of ivory, and it is adored; and it is no longer the god of a beast — and a most witless beast at that — but the supreme deity of the age: not because it is elephant, but because it is so great a Phidias. The living God, the true God — could He not have purged whatever cheapness of matter by His own working and healed it of all weakness? Or shall this remain — that a man should have fashioned a god more honourably than God fashioned a man? Now even though the slime be a stumbling-block, it is already another thing. I hold now flesh, not earth, although the flesh too hears: "Earth you are, and into earth you shall go." Its origin is recounted, its substance is not recalled. It has been granted to be something nobler than its origin and happier by its transformation. For gold too is earth, because it is from earth; yet only so far earth, from the point when it is gold — far other matter, more splendid and more noble out of a more worthless mother-lode. So it was permitted to God too to refine the gold of the flesh out of the slime — out of those dregs, as you think them — its worth being cleared.

But the authority of the flesh may seem weaker, because the divine hand did not handle it too, properly, as it did the slime. When He handled the slime to this end, that flesh should afterward be made of slime, He surely conducted the business of the flesh. But I would still have you learn when and how the flesh flowered out of the slime. For those skin tunics, which Adam and Eve, stripped of paradise, put on, will not be, as some would have it, the reshaping of flesh out of slime — since somewhat earlier Adam recognized, already in the woman, the offshoot of his own substance as flesh ("This now is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh"), and the very portion drawn off from the male was filled out into the female with flesh — to be filled out, I suppose, with slime, if Adam were still slime. The slime, then, was effaced and swallowed up into flesh. When? When man became a living soul by the breath of God — a vapour, that is, fit to bake the slime in some way into another quality, as if into a baked thing, so into flesh. So even the potter is permitted, by the controlled blast of fire, to re-embody the clay into a sturdier material and to draw out of one form another, fitter than the first and now of its own kind and name. For although it is written, "Shall the clay say to the potter?" — that is, man to God — and although the apostle says, "in vessels of clay" — yet man is clay, because he was slime before; and the flesh is earthenware, because it is from slime through the vapour of the divine breath, which afterward the skin tunics, that is, the over-drawn skins, clothed. So far is this so, that if you strip off the skin, you bare the flesh. Thus what today, if it be stripped off, becomes a spoil, was a garment when it was being built over. Hence the apostle too, calling circumcision a stripping-off of the flesh, affirmed the skin to be a tunic. Since these things are so, you have both the slime glorious from the hand of God, and the flesh more glorious from the breath of God, by which at once the flesh laid aside the rudiments of slime and took up the ornaments of the soul. You are not more careful than God: you, indeed, do not encase Scythian and Indian gems and the white grains of the Red Sea in lead or bronze or iron — no, nor even in silver — but you dig them about with the choicest and moreover most laboured gold; and likewise you first see to the fitness of the vessels for the most precious wines and unguents; and accordingly to swords of perfect temper you match a dignity of scabbards — and shall God have entrusted the shadow of His own soul, the breath of His own spirit, the work of His own mouth, to some most worthless sheath, and by setting it unworthily have surely condemned it? But did He set it, or rather insert and mingle it, with the flesh? — and that with so close a blending that it may be held uncertain whether the flesh carries the soul or the soul the flesh, whether the flesh appears to belong to the soul or the soul to the flesh. But it is rather to be believed that the soul is borne in and rules, as the nearer to God. This too overflows to the glory of the flesh, that it both contains what is nearest to God and renders it partaker of that very rule. For what use of nature, what fruit of the world, what savour of the elements does the soul feed upon except through the flesh? How not? — through which it is propped by every instrument of the senses, sight, hearing, taste, smell, touch; through which it is sprinkled with divine power, accomplishing nothing without speech, even when sent silently before. For speech too is from the organ of the flesh. The arts are through the flesh, the pursuits, the talents through the flesh, the works, the affairs, the duties through the flesh; and indeed the whole living of the soul belongs to the flesh, so that for the soul not to live is nothing else than to depart from the flesh. So too its very dying belongs to the flesh, whose also is its living. Further, if all things lie subject to the soul through the flesh, they lie subject to the flesh as well. That through which you make use of a thing, with that thing it is necessary that you make use. Thus the flesh, while it is accounted the minister and handmaid of the soul, is found to be its consort and co-heir. If of things temporal, why not of things eternal as well?

And these things I would have procured for the flesh, as it were, out of the common form of the human condition. Let us now see, even out of the special form of the Christian name, how great a prerogative this trifling and sordid substance has with God — although it would be enough for it that no soul at all can attain salvation unless, while it is in the flesh, it has believed; so much is the flesh the hinge of salvation. And when by it the soul is bound to God, it is the flesh itself that brings it about that the soul can be bound. For the flesh is washed, that the soul may be cleansed; the flesh is anointed, that the soul may be consecrated; the flesh is signed, that the soul too may be fortified; the flesh is overshadowed by the laying on of hands, that the soul too may be illumined by the Spirit; the flesh feeds on the body and blood of Christ, that the soul too may be fattened upon God. They cannot, then, be separated in their reward, whom their work joins together. For even the sacrifices acceptable to God — I mean the wrestlings of the soul, fastings and abstinences and dry meats and the squalor that is the appendage of this duty — the flesh undertakes out of its own discomfort. Virginity too, and widowhood, and the modest concealment of marriage in secret, and the sole knowledge of it, are offered to God out of the good things of the flesh. Come now, what do you think of it when, for the faith of the Name, it is dragged out into the open and publicly exposed to hatred and contends; when in prisons it is wasted by the most dismal exile from the light, by want of the world, by squalor, by filth, by the indignity of its fare, not even free in sleep — bound indeed even on its very couches and torn on the very straw; when now even in broad day it is mangled by every contrivance of torments; when at last it is paid out in punishments, striving to render Christ His due by dying for Him — and that often through the same cross, not to say through still more atrocious devices of penalties? Truly that flesh is most blessed and most glorious which can, before the Lord Christ, discharge so great a debt, so that it owes Him this alone — that it has ceased to owe Him — the more bound for being acquitted.

Therefore, to recapitulate: she whom God built with His own hands after the image of God; whom He animated from His own breath after the likeness of His own vitality; whom He set over the dwelling, the fruition, the lordship of His whole work; whom He clothed with His own sacraments and disciplines; whose cleannesses He loves, whose chastisements He approves, whose sufferings He prizes for Himself — shall she not rise again, she who dies so many times a day? Far be it, far be it that God should abandon to everlasting destruction the labour of His own hands, the care of His own genius, the sheath of His own breath, the queen of His own building, the heir of His own bounty, the priestess of His own religion, the soldier of His own testimony, the sister of His own Christ. We know a good God; that He is the only one, the best, we learn from His Christ — who, enjoining love, after His own toward our neighbour, will Himself also do what He has commanded. He will love the flesh, in so many ways near to Him: though it be weak, yet "Strength is perfected in weakness"; though it be sickly, yet "They that are whole need not a physician, but they that are ill"; though it be dishonourable, yet "Upon the more dishonourable parts we bestow the greater honour"; though it be lost, yet "I am come," He says, "to save that which was lost"; though it be sinful, yet "I prefer," He says, "the salvation of a sinner to his death"; though it be condemned, yet "I," He says, "will strike and will heal." Why do you cast up against the flesh those very things which await God, which hope in God, which are honoured by Him, to which He comes to aid? I would dare to say: if these things had not befallen the flesh, the kindness, the grace, the mercy, all the beneficent power of God would have been idle.

You hold the Scriptures by which the flesh is darkened; hold also those by which it is lighted. You read where it is put down; turn your eyes also to where it is unveiled. "All flesh is grass." Not this only did Isaiah pronounce, but also, "All flesh shall see the salvation of God." It is noted in Genesis that God says, "My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh." But it is also heard through Joel: "I will pour out of My spirit upon all flesh." The apostle too — do not know him by one pen only, with which he often pricks the flesh. For although he denies that anything good dwells in his flesh, although he affirms that those who are in the flesh cannot please God, because it lusts against the spirit, and though he sets down certain other things in such a way that not the substance but the act of the flesh is dishonoured — we shall indeed say elsewhere that nothing ought properly to be cast up against the flesh except to the reproach of the soul, which subdues the flesh to itself for its ministry. But meanwhile, even in those writings, there is the Paul who carries the marks of Christ in his body; who forbids our body, as God's temple, to be defiled; who makes our bodies members of Christ; who admonishes us to bear and to magnify God in our body. And so, if the ignominies of the flesh shut out its resurrection, why should not its dignities rather bring it in? Since it is more in keeping with God to recall unto salvation what He has sometimes reproved, than to deliver unto perdition what He has even sometimes approved.

Thus far concerning the proclamation of the flesh against its enemies — and yet its closest friends. For no one lives so carnally as those who deny the resurrection of the flesh. For in denying it they despise both punishment and discipline. Of whom the Paraclete too speaks luminously through the prophetess Prisca: "They are flesh, and they hate the flesh." But if so great an authority fortifies the flesh as can plead for it toward the merit of salvation, must we not also rehearse the very power and might and freedom of God Himself — whether He is great enough to avail to rebuild and restore the tabernacle of the flesh, fallen apart and devoured and snatched away by whatever means? And whether He has promulgated for us some examples too of this His own right in the public realm of nature — lest perhaps any still thirst to know God, who is to be believed on no other ground than that He is believed able to do all things? Plainly, among the philosophers you have those who defend this world as unborn and unmade; but far better is it that nearly all the heresies, granting the world to be born and made, ascribe its creation to our God. Be confident, then, that He brought forth this whole out of nothing, and you know God by being confident of this — that only God avails so much. For some of the weaker sort prefer to believe this first about matter — they wish the universe to have been dedicated by Him out of underlying matter, after the philosophers. Yet even if it were so held in truth, since He would still be said to have brought forth substances far other, and species far other, out of the reshaping of matter, than the matter itself had been — I should none the less maintain that He brought them forth out of nothing, if He had brought forth things that had not existed at all. For what does it matter whether a thing be brought forth out of nothing or out of something, provided that what was not comes to be — since even to have not been is as good as to be nothing? So, conversely, to have been is as good as to be something. Now, even though it matters, yet either way it applauds my case. For whether God built all things out of nothing, He will be able to express the flesh too, reduced to nothing, out of nothing; or whether He shaped all things out of other matter, He will be able to call forth the flesh too, drained away whither it will, out of something else. And surely He is fit to remake who made — by how much it is more to have made than to have remade, to have given a beginning than to have given back. So you may believe the restoration of the flesh easier than its institution.

Look now also at the very examples of the divine power. Day dies into night, and is everywhere buried in darkness. The honour of the world is laid in mourning; all substance is blackened. All things grow sordid, silent, stupefied; everywhere there is a cessation, a rest of things. So the lost light is lamented. And yet again, with its own adornment, with its dowry, with the sun, the same light, whole and entire, comes back to life for the whole world — slaying its own death, the night, rending its own grave, the darkness, becoming heir to itself, until the night too comes back to life with its own retinue. For the rays of the stars too are rekindled, which the morning's burning had quenched; the absences of the constellations are brought back, which the distinction of the seasons had removed; the mirrors of the moon are restored, which the monthly count had worn away. Winters and summers, springs and autumns roll round again, with their own forces, characters, fruits. Indeed, even the earth receives discipline from heaven: to clothe the trees again after their spoils, to colour the flowers anew, to set out the grasses once more, to exhibit the same seeds that had been consumed — and not to exhibit them before they are consumed. Wonderful reckoning: out of a defrauder, a preserver; to give back, it intercepts; to keep, it loses; to make whole, it spoils; even to enlarge, it first wastes away. For it restores things richer and more cultivated than it had banished — truly with destruction for interest, with injury for usury, with loss for gain. Let me say it once: the whole creation is recurrent. Whatever you meet with, has been; whatever you lose, is nothing if not again. All things return to their state when they have departed; all things begin when they have ceased; for this reason they end, that they may come to be. Nothing perishes but unto salvation. This whole revolving order of things, then, is a witness to the resurrection of the dead. God has prescribed it by His works before He prescribed it by His letters; He has proclaimed it by His powers before by His words. He has sent ahead Nature as your mistress, about to send under her also prophecy — that you may the more easily believe prophecy, being a disciple of nature; that you may admit it at once, when you have heard what you have already everywhere seen; nor doubt that God is the raiser of the flesh too, whom you have known to be the restorer of all things. And surely, if all things rise again for man, for whom they were provided — and they were provided not for man unless for the flesh as well — how is it that the flesh itself should perish utterly, for whose sake, and to whom, nothing perishes?

If the universe figures the resurrection too little, if the creation signifies nothing of the kind — because its single things are said not so much to die as to cease, and are thought not to be re-animated but reshaped — receive the fullest and firmest specimen of this hope, since it is a living thing, subject to life and to death: I mean that bird peculiar to the East, famous for its singularity, monstrous for its posterity — which willingly burying itself renews itself, departing by a natal end and succeeding, again a phoenix where now there is none, again the same which is now no more, another the same. What is more expressive and more significant for this cause, or to what other matter is there such a proof? God also in His Scriptures says, "And he shall flower like a phoenix" — that is, out of death, out of the funeral — that you may believe that the substance of the body can be required even from the fires. The Lord pronounced that we are of more worth than many sparrows; if not also than the phoenixes, it is no great thing. But shall men perish once for all, while the birds of Arabia are secure of resurrection?

With such lineaments of the divine powers meanwhile — God having wrought no less in parables than in speech — let us come also to His very edicts and decrees, by which most of all we now arrange this division of our subject. For we have begun from the authority of the flesh, whether it be such as salvation befits when it has fallen apart; then we have followed on concerning the power of God, whether it be such as is wont to confer salvation upon a thing fallen apart. Now, if we have proved both, I would have you ask also about the cause — whether there be any cause so worthy as may vindicate the resurrection of the flesh as necessary and certainly in every way due to reason; for it remains to be said that, even though the flesh be capable of being restored, even though the divinity be fit to restore, yet a cause of restoration ought to take precedence. Receive, then, the cause too, you who learn that with God there is the best as well as the just — the best from His own part, the just from ours. For had not man sinned, he would have known God as the best only, out of the property of His nature. But now he experiences Him also as just, out of the necessity of the case — yet by this very thing the best, while He is also just. For by aiding the good and punishing the evil, exhibiting justice in both sentences, He serves the good: here vindicating this, there rewarding that. But with Marcion you will learn more fully whether this be the whole of God. Meanwhile such is our God: rightly a judge, because Lord; rightly Lord, because Author; rightly Author, because God. Hence also that, I know not who, of the heretics is rightly no judge, for he is no lord; rightly no lord, for he is no author; I know not now whether he is even God, who is neither author (which God is) nor lord (which the author is). Therefore, if to God and Lord and Author it is most fitting to appoint judgment upon man concerning this very thing — whether he has cared to acknowledge and observe his Lord and Author or not — the resurrection too will discharge that judgment. This will be the whole cause, nay the necessity, of the resurrection: the appointment of judgment, most fitting, of course, to God. And concerning the disposition of that judgment you may consider whether the divine censure presides over both substances of man, to be judged — the soul as well as the flesh. For what it shall befit to be judged, this it will be fit also to be raised again. We say that the judgment of God is to be believed full and perfect from the first — as being now final and thenceforth perpetual; so being also just, while it is in nothing less; so being also worthy of God, while, for so great a patience of His, it is full and perfect. And so the fullness and perfection of judgment can consist of nothing but the representation of the whole man; the whole man, further, comes of the concretion of both substances; and therefore he is to be exhibited in both, whom it behoves to be judged as a whole — who, unless whole, has certainly not lived at all. As, then, he has lived, so is he to be judged, because he has to be judged concerning that whereby he has lived. For life is the cause of judgment, to be discharged through as many substances as it has also been performed through.

Come now, let our adversaries cut the joining of flesh and soul first in the administration of life, that so they may dare to cut it also in the rewarding of life. Let them deny a partnership of works, that they may justly be able also to deny a partnership of wage. Let the flesh have no share in the sentence, if it had none also in the cause. Let the soul alone be recalled, if it alone departs. But indeed it no more departs alone than it ran alone the course from which it departs — this present life, I mean. And so far is it from being the soul alone that transacts life, that we cannot remove even thoughts — though they be solitary, though not carried through into effect by the flesh — from the partnership of the flesh; since whatever is done in the heart is done by the soul in the flesh and with the flesh and through the flesh. This very seat of the flesh, the citadel of the soul, the Lord too marks for the reproof of thoughts: "Why do you think evil in your hearts?" and: "Whoever has looked upon a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery in his heart." So far is the thought, even without work and without effect, an act of the flesh. But even if in the brain, or in the midpoint between the brows, or wheresoever it pleases the philosophers, the principality of the senses has been consecrated — what is called the HEGEMONIKON — the whole place of the soul's thinking will be flesh. The soul is never without the flesh so long as it is in the flesh. There is nothing it does not do with that without which it does not exist. Ask still further whether thoughts too are administered through the flesh, which are discerned through the flesh from without. Let the soul revolve something, and the countenance works the index of it; the face is the mirror of all intentions. Let them deny a partnership of deeds to that to which they cannot deny a partnership of thoughts. And they indeed enumerate the delinquencies of the flesh: therefore as a sinner it will be held liable to punishment. But we, on the other hand, set against these the virtues of the flesh: therefore, as having wrought well, it will be held entitled to reward. And if it is the soul that acts and impels toward all things, it is the compliance of the flesh. God may not be believed either an unjust judge or an inert one: unjust, if He shut out from rewards the partner of good works; inert, if He sever from punishments the partner of evil ones — since even human judgment is held the more perfect the more it demands also the ministers of each deed, neither sparing nor envying them, but admitting them to share with the doers the fruit of either penalty or favour.

But when we assign the command to the soul and compliance to the flesh, we must take heed lest by another line of argument they overturn even this — wishing so to set the flesh in the office of the soul, not as a minister, that from this they may not be forced to acknowledge it as a partner. For they will say that ministers and partners have the choice of ministering and partnering and the power of their own will toward either — being themselves men, namely — and that therefore they share merits with the doers, to whom they lend their labour of their own accord; but that the flesh, knowing nothing, feeling nothing of itself, having of its own no willing or unwilling, appears rather as a vessel of the soul, as an instrument, not as a ministry. And so the judgment presides over the soul alone — how it has used the vessel of the flesh — while the vessel itself is not liable to the sentence; just as a cup is not condemned if a man has tempered it with poison, nor a sword sentenced to the beasts if a man has done a robbery with it. The flesh, then, is now innocent in that part wherein those evil works will not be reckoned to it, and nothing forbids that it be made safe under the name of innocence. For although good works are not reckoned to it, just as neither are evil, yet it is the more fitting to the divine kindness to set free the innocent. For He who is beneficent owes it; but it belongs to the best to offer even what is not owed. And yet a cup — I do not say a poison-cup, into which some death has belched, but one infected with the breath of a harlot or an arch-eunuch or a gladiator or an executioner — I ask, would you condemn it less than their very kisses? Even one clouded with our own filth, or not tempered to our liking, we are wont to dash down, so as to be the more angry with the slave. But a sword drunk with robberies — who would not banish it from the whole house, much more from the bedchamber, much more from the service of his own head — presuming, of course, that he would dream of nothing else than the mockings of souls, the souls that press and disquiet him, the bedfellow of his own blood? But on the other hand, a cup well conscious of itself, commended for the diligence of its service, will be adorned even with its drinker's garlands or honoured with a sprinkling of flowers. And a sword nobly bloodied in war, the better for being a slayer, will pay its praise with consecration. There is, then, a fixing of the sentence even upon vessels and upon instruments, so that they too share in the merits of their masters and doers — that I may have satisfied this argument too, although the difference of things lacks the support of the example. For every vessel or instrument comes into use from elsewhere, of matter wholly foreign to the substance of man. But the flesh, sown together from the beginning of the womb, formed together, born together with the soul, is mingled with it in every operation too. For although it is called a vessel in the apostle, which he bids be handled in honour, yet the same thing is by the same man called the outer man — that slime, namely, which was first inscribed with the title of man, not of a cup or a sword or any vessel. For it is called a vessel by reason of capacity, by which it holds and contains the soul; but man by reason of the fellowship of nature, which renders it not an instrument in operations but a ministry. So the ministry too will be held liable to judgment, even if it knows nothing of its own, because it is a portion of that which knows, not a piece of furniture. This too the apostle, knowing that the flesh does nothing of itself which is not also reckoned to the soul, none the less judges the flesh a sinner, lest, by being seen to be impelled by the soul, it be believed freed from judgment. So too, when he enjoins certain works of praise upon the flesh — "Glorify," he says, "and bear up God in your body" — certain though he is that this endeavour too is wrought by the soul, yet he commands it also of the flesh, because to it too he promises in turn the fruit. Otherwise neither would reproach have fitted upon another's fault, nor exhortation upon another's glory; for both reproach and exhortation toward the flesh would be idle, if the wage were idle that is grasped at in the resurrection.

Every simpler supporter of our view will think that the flesh must on this account too be presented to judgment, because otherwise the soul, being incorporeal, would not be capable of the suffering of torment or of refreshment; for so the crowd thinks. But we both profess here and prove in its own volume that the soul is corporeal, having its own kind of substance of solidity, through which it can both feel and suffer anything. For that even now souls are tortured and cherished among the dead — though naked, though as yet exiles from the flesh — the example of Lazarus will prove. I have therefore allowed the adversary to say: "Then that which has its own corpulence will suffice of itself for the faculty of suffering and feeling, so that it has no need of the presentation of the flesh." Nay rather, it will have need so far as this: not in that it cannot feel anything without the flesh, but in that it is necessary that it feel even with the flesh. For as far as it suffices of itself for acting, so far also for suffering. But for acting it suffices less of itself. For it has of its own only to think, to will, to desire, to dispose. But for completing the work it waits upon the flesh. So therefore for suffering too it requires the partnership of the flesh, that it may be able to suffer as fully through it as it could not, without it, fully act. And therefore in those things for which it suffices of itself — concupiscence and thought and will — it meanwhile pays the sentence of them. Further, if these were enough for the fullness of merits, so that deeds too were not required, the soul would suffice wholly for the perfection of judgment, to be judged concerning those things for which acting it alone had sufficed. But since deeds too are bound up with merits, and deeds are administered through the flesh, now it is not enough that the soul be cherished or tortured without the flesh even for the works of the flesh — though it have a body, though it have members, which accordingly do not suffice it for feeling fully, just as not for acting perfectly. Therefore, in whatever manner it has acted, for that it also suffers among the dead, tasting judgment beforehand, as it brought in beforehand the offence; yet waiting also for the flesh, that through it too it may make compensation for the deeds, to which it had entrusted the things thought. In short, this will be the reason of the judgment appointed for the uttermost end: that by the exhibition of the flesh the whole divine censure may be accomplished. Otherwise that which even now the souls pluck among the dead would not be sustained unto the end, if it were appointed to souls alone.

Thus far I have wrought with foundation-layings to fortify the senses of all the Scriptures which promise the return of the flesh. For which, since so many authorities of just patronages provide — I mean the honours of the very substance, then the powers of God, then the examples of them, then the reasons of the judgment and its necessities — surely the Scriptures will have to be understood according to the prejudgments of so many authorities, not according to the inventions of the heretics, which come from mere incredulity, because it is held incredible that a substance withdrawn by destruction should be restored — not because it is either unmeritable to the substance itself, or impossible to God, or unfit for judgment. Plainly it would be incredible, had it not been foretold by God; except that, even if it had not been foretold by Him, it ought of its own accord to be presumed — so that on that account it was not foretold, because it was prejudged by so many authorities. But since it resounds also with divine voices, so far is it from being understood otherwise than they desire by whom it is proved even without the divine voices. Let us see, then, this first: by what title this hope has been proscribed. One edict of God, I think, hangs upon the mind of all: "The resurrection of the dead." Two words, ready, decisive, clear-cut. These same I will engage, these I will discuss — to which substance they make themselves over. When I hear that resurrection is impending upon man, I must of necessity ask what part of him has been allotted to fall; since nothing will look for rising again except what has first fallen down. He who does not know that the flesh falls through death can know it neither as standing through life. Nature pronounces God's sentence: "Earth you are, and into earth you shall go." And he who has not heard it, sees it. There is no death that is not a ruin of the members. This lot of the body the Lord too expressed, when, clothed in that very substance, He said, "Destroy this temple, and I in three days will raise it up again." For He showed whose it is to be destroyed, whose to be dashed down, whose to lie low, whose also to be lifted up and raised again — although He bore about also a soul trembling even unto death, but not falling through death; for the Scripture too had said, "He had spoken concerning His body." And so far is it the flesh that is overthrown by death, that thereafter from its falling it is called a "corpse." But the soul falls not even in name, because it sinks not even in posture. And yet it is itself that brings ruin upon the body when it is breathed out, just as it is itself that will raise it up from the earth when it has entered. That cannot fall which will raise up by entering; that cannot sink which dashes down by going forth. I will say it more strictly: the soul does not fall even into sleep with the body, nor is it even then laid low with the flesh. For it is agitated and tossed about in dreams; but it would be quiet if it lay, and would lie if it fell. So it falls not into the reality of death, since it sinks not even into its image. Now examine likewise the following word, "of the dead," on what substance it sits; although in this matter we may sometimes grant that mortality is assigned to the soul by the heretics, so that, if a mortal soul is to attain resurrection, there is a prejudgment also for the flesh, no less mortal, which is to share in resurrection. But for now the propriety of the word must be vindicated to its own lot. Already indeed by this very thing — that resurrection belongs to a fallen thing, that is, to the flesh — the same will hold also in the name "dead," because resurrection belongs to a fallen thing, which is called "of the dead." So too through Abraham, the father of faith, we learn a man of divine familiarity. For asking of the sons of Heth a place for the burial of Sarah, "Give me, then," he says, "a possession of a sepulchre among you, and I will bury my dead" — the flesh, namely. For he would not have desired space for the burial of a soul, even were the soul believed mortal, even did it deserve to be called "dead." But if "dead" is the body, the resurrection will be of bodies, when it is said "of the dead."

And so this examination of the title and of the proclamation itself, defending the faith of the words, must avail to this: that, if the opposing party throws anything into confusion under the cover of figures and riddles, the clearer passages may prevail, and prescribe the more certain things concerning the uncertain. For some, having lit upon the most customary form of prophetic speech — allegorical and figurative for the most part, yet not always — twist even the resurrection of the dead, manifestly announced, into an imaginary signification, asserting that even death itself is to be understood spiritually. For that this is not the true death which lies in the midst, the parting of flesh and soul, but ignorance of God, through which a man dead to God has lain in error no less than in a sepulchre. And so the resurrection too is to be claimed as that by which a man, having approached the truth, re-animated and re-quickened, the death of ignorance shaken off, has burst forth as from the sepulchre of the old man — because the Lord too likened the scribes and Pharisees to whitened sepulchres. Thence, then, having attained resurrection by faith, they are with the Lord when they have put Him on in baptism. By this device, in short, they are wont often to deceive our people even in conversations, as though they too admit the resurrection of the flesh. "Woe," they say, "to him who shall not have risen in this flesh," lest they strike them at once, if they at once deny the resurrection. But silently, according to their own conscience, they mean this: "Woe to him who, while he is in this flesh, shall not have known the heretical secrets" — for this is, with them, the resurrection. But very many, too, claiming resurrection from the departure of the soul, interpret "to go out of the sepulchre" as "to escape from the world," because the world too is the dwelling of the dead, that is, of those ignorant of God; or even from the body itself, because the body too detains the soul, shut up as in a sepulchre, in the death of worldly life.

On account, then, of conjectures of this kind, I will drive away their first foundation-laying, by which they will have it that the prophets harangued everything by images — since, were it so, not even the images themselves could have been distinguished, had not the truths also been proclaimed from which the images would be sketched. And indeed, if all things are figures, what will that be of which they are figures? How will you hold out a mirror, if there is nowhere a face? But so far are not all things images, but truths also, nor all shadows, but bodies also, that even concerning the Lord Himself the more remarkable things were proclaimed clearer than light. For the Virgin conceived in her womb not figuratively, and bore Emmanuel, "God with us," Jesus, not obliquely; and if obliquely, that "He should receive the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria" — yet manifestly, that "He should come for judgment with the elders and princes of the people." For the nations were in tumult in the person of Pilate, and the peoples meditated vain things in the person of Israel. "The kings of the earth stood up" — Herod — "and the rulers were gathered together into one" — Annas and Caiaphas — "against the Lord and against His Christ." Who also was led "as a sheep to the slaughter," and "as a lamb before its shearer" — Herod, namely — "without voice; so He opened not His mouth"; giving His back to the scourges, and His cheeks to the palms, and turning not His face from the darts of spittings; reckoned also among the wicked, His hands and feet pierced, suffering a casting of lots over His garment, and bitter draughts, and the noddings of mocking heads, valued at thirty pieces of silver by the betrayer. What are these figures in Isaiah, what images in David, what riddles in Jeremiah — when not even His mighty works were uttered through parables? Or were the eyes of the blind not opened, nor the tongue of the dumb made clear, nor the withered hands and loosened knees made strong again, nor the lame leaped like a hart? Which things, although we are wont to interpret spiritually too, according to the comparison of the vices of the soul healed by the Lord, yet since they were fulfilled carnally as well, show that the prophets prophesied in both kinds — saving the fact that very many of their voices can be defended as bare and simple and pure of every cloud of allegory: as when the downfalls of nations and cities resound — of Tyre and Egypt and Babylon and Idumaea and the ships of the Carthaginians — as when they speak through to the end of Israel's own plagues or pardons, captivities, restorations, and the issue of the final dispersion. Who will interpret these rather than recognize them? Things are held in the letters as the letters are read in the things. So the form of prophetic speech is not always nor in all things allegorical, but sometimes and in certain things.

"If, then, sometimes and in certain things," you say, "why not also in the edict of resurrection, to be understood spiritually?" Because a very great reason intervenes. For first, what will so many and such divine documents do, so openly attesting a bodily resurrection that they admit no suspicion of figured signification? And surely it would be fair — as we charged above too — that uncertain things be prejudged from certain, and obscure from manifest; lest, amid the discord of the certain and the uncertain, the manifest and the obscure, faith be dissipated, truth imperilled, the very divinity branded as inconstant. Then, because it is not likely that that form of the sacrament into which all faith is committed, upon which all discipline strives, should appear ambiguously announced and obscurely set forth — since the hope of resurrection, unless manifest concerning peril and reward, would persuade no one to a religion of this kind especially, liable to public hatred and a hostile sentence. No work is sure for an uncertain wage. No fear is just of a doubtful peril. But both the wage and the peril hang upon the event of the resurrection. And further, if temporal and local and personal decrees and judgments of God upon cities and nations and kings were hurled by prophecy so openly, how is it that His eternal and universal dispositions upon the whole race of men should have fled their own light? — which, the greater they are, the clearer they ought to be, that the greater things may be believed. And I think that neither spite nor guile nor inconstancy nor enticement can be ascribed to God, by which for the most part the promulgation of greater matters is cavilled at.

After these things we must look back also to those Scriptures which do not allow the resurrection, according to these soul-bound — not to say spiritual — men, either to be presumed already here in the recognition of the truth, or to be claimed immediately upon the departure of life. For since the times of the whole hope have been fixed by the sacrosanct pen, and it is not lawful for it to be established before the coming, I think, of Christ — our prayers sigh for the setting of this present age, for the passing of the world too unto the great day of the Lord, the day of wrath and retribution, the last and hidden day, known to none but the Father, and yet foremarked by signs and portents and shakings of the elements and conflicts of nations. I would unroll the prophecies, had the Lord Himself been silent (except that the prophecies too were the voice of the Lord); but it is more that He sets His seal to them with His own mouth. Asked by His disciples when those things would come to pass which He had meanwhile burst forth concerning the temple's downfall, He sets in order, first, the times of the Jews up to the destruction of Jerusalem, then, of the common things, up to the conclusion of the age. For after He had declared, "And then Jerusalem shall be trodden down by the nations, until the times of the nations be fulfilled" — those, namely, to be enrolled by God and gathered with the remnants of Israel — thence already, unto the world and unto the age, He proclaims, according to Joel and Daniel and the whole council of the prophets, signs to come in the sun and in the moon and in the stars, a clashing of nations with amazement at the sound of the sea, and the failing of men growing cold for fear and expectation of those things which threaten the world. "For the powers of the heavens," He says, "shall be shaken; and then they shall see the Son of Man coming in the clouds, with great power and glory. But when these things shall begin to come to pass, look up, and lift up your heads, for your redemption draws near." And yet He said that it draws near, not that it is already present; and "when these things shall begin to come to pass," not "when they shall have been done" — because when they shall have been done, then our redemption will be present, which is said to draw near only so far, meanwhile raising and rousing our minds to the now-nearest fruit of hope. Of which a parable too is woven in, of the trees growing tender into the stalk of the flower, and the flower thereafter the forerunner of the fruit. "So you also, when you shall see all these things come to pass, know that the kingdom of God is near. Watch, therefore, at all times, that you may be held worthy to escape all these things, and to stand before the Son of Man" — surely through resurrection, all things being transacted before. So, although it sprouts in the recognition of the sacrament, yet it flowers and bears fruit in the presentation of the Lord. Who, then, has roused the Lord so unseasonably, so harshly — He being already at the right hand of God — to crush the earth according to Isaiah, which, I think, is still whole? Who has already subjected the enemies of Christ beneath His feet according to David — as if swifter than the Father — while still the whole assembly of the populace cries out, "The Christians to the lion"? Who has beheld Jesus descending from heaven, such as the apostles had seen Him ascending, according to the appointment of the angels? No tribes have to this day fallen breast to breast, recognizing Him whom they pierced. No one has yet received Elijah; no one has yet fled the antichrist; no one has yet wept the downfall of Babylon. And is there already one who has risen, except a heretic? Plainly he has already gone forth from the sepulchre of his body — even now liable to fevers and ulcers; and he has already trodden down his enemies — even now having to wrestle with the powers of the world. And surely he already reigns — even now owing to Caesar the things that are Caesar's.

The apostle indeed teaches, writing to the Colossians, that we were once dead, alienated and enemies in mind to the Lord, when we were busy in the worst works; then buried together with Christ in baptism, and raised together in Him through faith in the working of God, who raised Him from the dead. "And you, when you were dead in your offences and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, He quickened together with Him, having forgiven you all offences." And again: "If you are dead with Christ from the elements of the world, why, as though living in the world, do you pass sentence?" But while He thus makes us dead spiritually, yet so as to acknowledge that we shall sometime die corporeally too, surely He, deeming us likewise raised again spiritually, equally does not deny that we shall rise corporeally too. In short, "If you have risen with Christ," he says, "seek the things that are above, where Christ sits at the right hand of God; mind the things that are above, not those that are below." So he shows that we rise in mind, by which alone as yet we can touch heavenly things — which we should not seek nor mind, if we possessed them. He adds also: "For you are dead" — to your offences, namely, not to yourselves — "and your life is hidden with Christ in God." Not yet, then, has it been laid hold of, which is hidden. So John too: "And it is not yet manifest," he says, "what we shall be. We know that, if He shall be manifested, we shall be like Him." So far are we from being already that which we know not — yet about to know it, were we already it. So far is it a contemplation of hope, in this span, through faith — not a presentation, nor a possession, but an expectation. Of which hope and expectation Paul to the Galatians: "For we through the spirit, from faith, expect the hope of righteousness" — he does not say "hold." "Of the righteousness of God" he speaks, from the judgment by which we shall be judged concerning the wage. Hanging upon which he himself too writes to the Philippians: "If by any means," he says, "I may attain unto the resurrection which is from the dead — not because I have already received, or am consummated." And surely he had believed, and had known all the sacraments, the vessel of election, the teacher of the nations; and yet he adds: "But I follow after, if I may lay hold, of that in which I am laid hold of by Christ." Yet more: "I, brethren, do not count myself to have laid hold; but one thing — forgetting the things behind, stretching myself toward the things before, according to the mark I follow after, unto the palm of accusation, through which I might attain" — surely unto the raising up from the dead, yet in its own time, as to the Galatians: "But in well-doing let us not be weary; for in its own time we shall reap." As also to Timothy concerning Onesiphorus: "May the Lord grant him to find mercy in that day." Unto which day and time he commands him too to keep the commandment immaculate, irreproachable, "unto the appearing of the Lord Jesus Christ, which in His own times He shall show, the blessed and only potentate, and King of kings, and Lord of lords" — speaking of God. Of which times Peter too in the Acts: "Repent, therefore, and be converted, for the blotting out of your offences, that the times of refreshment may come upon you from the presence of God, and He may send the Christ foredesigned for you, whom the heavens must receive until the times of the restitution of all things which God has spoken by the mouth of His holy prophets."

What these times are, learn with the Thessalonians. For we read: "How you turned from idols to serve the living and true God, and to await from the heavens His Son, whom He raised from the dead, Jesus." And again: "For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of exultation — except even you, before our Lord God Jesus Christ, in His coming?" Likewise: "Before God and our Father, in the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, with all His saints." Teaching them to mourn the less for the sleep of these, he at the same time sets forth the times of the resurrection, saying: "For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with Him those who have slept through Jesus. For this we say to you in the word of the Lord, that we who live, who remain unto the coming of our Lord, shall not anticipate those who have slept. For the Lord Himself, at the command and at the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God, shall descend from heaven; and the dead in Christ shall rise first; then we who live, who shall together with them be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air; and so shall we ever be with the Lord." What voice of the archangel, what trumpet of God has been heard already — unless perhaps in the bedchambers of the heretics? For although the trumpet of God may be called the evangelic word, which would already call them — yet either they will already be corporeally dead, so as to have risen, and how do they live? or caught up into the clouds, and how are they here? Most wretched indeed, as the apostle pronounced, who will be held as hoping in this life only — to be shut out, while they snatch beforehand what is promised after that life — frustrated about the truth, no less than Phygellus and Hermogenes. And therefore the majesty of the Holy Spirit, perceptive of such notions, suggests even in the same epistle to the Thessalonians: "But of the times and the spaces of times, brethren, there is no need to write to you. For you yourselves know most surely that the day of the Lord shall come as a thief in the night. When they shall say, Peace, and All things are safe, then sudden destruction shall fall upon them." And in the second, with fuller solicitude, to the same: "But I beseech you, brethren, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together unto Him, that you be not soon moved in mind, nor troubled, neither by spirit, nor by word" — of pseudo-prophets, namely — "nor by epistle" — of pseudo-apostles, namely — "as though by ours, as if the day of the Lord were at hand. Let no one deceive you in any way. For unless there come first the falling away" — of this kingdom, surely — "and the man of delinquency be revealed, that is, the antichrist, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God or religion, so that he sits in the temple of God, affirming himself to be God. Do you not remember that, when I was with you, I told you these things? And now you know what restrains, that he may be revealed in his own time. For already the mystery of iniquity is at work; only let him who now restrains restrain, until he be removed out of the way." Who, except the Roman state, whose falling away, dispersed into ten kings, shall bring on the antichrist? "And then the wicked one shall be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus shall slay with the spirit of His mouth, and shall make void by the manifestation of His coming — whose coming is according to the working of Satan, in all power and signs and lying portents, and in all the seduction of unrighteousness, to those who perish."

In the Apocalypse of John too the order of times is laid out, which even the souls of the martyrs under the altar, demanding vengeance and judgment, have learned to endure: that first the world too may drink down its plagues from the bowls of the angels, and that prostituted city receive from ten kings its worthy downfalls, and the beast antichrist, with his pseudo-prophet, wage war against the church of God; and so, the devil meanwhile relegated into the abyss, the prerogative of the first resurrection be ordered from thrones; thereafter, fire being given, by the censure of the universal resurrection judgment be passed out of the books. Since, therefore, the Scriptures both note the state of the last times and place the whole fruit of Christian hope at the going-out of the age, it appears either that then is fulfilled all whatsoever is promised us by God — and what is here already claimed by the heretics is empty; or, if even the recognition of the sacrament is resurrection, surely that is believed safe which is proclaimed at the last; and it follows that by this very thing, by which this spiritual one is claimed, that bodily one is prejudged. For if none were announced for then, rightly would this alone, and only the spiritual, be claimed. But since one is decreed even for the last time, the bodily one is acknowledged, because the spiritual one is not announced for then too. For why should a resurrection of the same condition — that is, spiritual — be announced a second time, when it ought either now to be discharged without any difference of times, or then, under every closing of times? So it is the more fitting for us to defend even the spiritual resurrection from the entry of faith, who acknowledge its fullness at the going-out of the age.

One thing more I will answer to the former proposition concerning allegorical Scriptures: that it is lawful for us too to claim the bodily resurrection from the patronage of likewise figured prophetic speech. For behold, the divine sentence at the beginning, pronouncing man to be earth — "Earth you are, and into earth you shall go," according to the substance of the flesh, namely, which had been taken from the earth, and which had first been called man, as we have shown — gives me a discipline of interpreting into the flesh too, if God has established anything of wrath or grace upon the earth; because the earth is not properly liable to His judgment, having admitted nothing of good or evil. Cursed indeed is the earth that drinks blood — but this too into a figure of the homicide flesh. For even if the earth is to be helped or harmed, that too is on account of man, that he be helped or harmed through the downfalls of his own consistory; the more shall he weigh what the earth too suffers on his account. And so, when God threatens the earth, I will say that He threatens the flesh rather; and when He promises anything to the earth, I will understand that He promises to the flesh rather, as in David: "The Lord has reigned; let the earth exult" — that is, the flesh of the saints, to which the fruit of the divine kingdom pertains. Then he subjoins: "He looked, and the earth was shaken; the mountains were melted like wax from the face of the Lord" — the flesh of the profane, namely; and, "For they shall see Him whom they pierced." And indeed, if both will be thought pronounced simply of the earth as an element, how will it fit that it be both shaken and melted from the face of the Lord, at whose reigning above it exulted? So too in Isaiah: "You shall eat the good things of the earth" — the good things of the flesh shall be understood, which await it reformed in the kingdom of God and made angelic, and about to attain those things "which neither eye has seen nor ear heard, nor have they ascended into the heart of man." Otherwise it is vain enough that God should invite to obedience by the fruits of the field and the foods of this life, which He shares, by a condition once assigned to man, even with the irreligious and the blasphemers — "raining upon the good and the evil, and sending His sun upon the just and the unjust." A happy faith indeed, if it is to attain those things which the enemies of God and of Christ not only use but even abuse, worshipping the very creation against the Creator! Will you reckon bulbs and tubers among the good things of the earth, when the Lord pronounces that man shall not live by bread alone? So the Jews, by hoping for earthly things only, lose the heavenly — ignorant both of the bread promised from heaven, and of the oil of divine anointing, and the wine of the spirit, the water of the soul made vigorous from the vine of Christ. Just as they reckon the very holy land to be properly the Jewish soil, which is rather to be interpreted of the flesh of the Lord, which thereafter is holy land in all who have put on Christ — truly holy by the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, truly flowing with milk and honey by the sweetness of the hope itself, truly Jewish by familiarity with God. "For he is not a Jew who is so in the open, but who is so in secret." So that the temple of God may be the same, and Jerusalem, hearing from Isaiah, "Arise, arise, Jerusalem, put on the strength of your arm. Arise, as in the beginning of the day" — that is, in that integrity which had been before the offence of transgression. For what voices of exhortation and summons of this kind would fit upon that Jerusalem which killed the prophets and stoned those sent to her, and at last pierced her own Lord? But neither is salvation promised to any earth at all, which must pass away with the fashion of the whole world. Even if anyone will dare to argue the holy land to be paradise rather, which it may also receive to be called the land of the fathers — of Adam and Eve, namely — then likewise a restitution into paradise will seem promised to the flesh, which was allotted to dwell in it and keep it, so that such a man be recalled thither as was driven thence.

We have also mention of garments in the Scriptures to allegorize to the hope of the flesh, since the Apocalypse of John too says, "These are they who have not defiled their garments with women" — signifying virgins, namely, and those who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven. And so they shall be in white garments, that is, in the brightness of unwedded flesh. And in the Gospel the wedding garment can be recognized as the sanctity of the flesh. And so Isaiah, teaching what kind of fast the Lord has chosen, when he subjoins concerning the reward of goodness, "Then," he says, "your light shall break forth in due season, and your garments shall sooner spring up" — not silk, surely, nor a cloak, but wishing the flesh to be understood, he proclaimed the springing up of the flesh that is to rise from the setting of death. So far does an allegorical defence of the bodily resurrection lie at hand for us too. For even when we read, "My people, enter into your storehouses for a little while, until my wrath pass over" — the storehouses will be the sepulchres, in which they shall have to rest a little who in the borders of the age, under the last wrath, shall have departed through the force of the antichrist. Or why has he used the term "storehouses" rather, and not of some place of reception, except because in storehouses the salted flesh, laid up for use, is kept, to be brought forth thence in its own time? For likewise bodies too, prepared with the condiments of burial, are sequestered in mausoleums and monuments, to go forth thence when the Lord shall command. Which, since it fits to be so understood — for what refuges of storehouses shall keep us from the wrath of God? — by this very thing, that he says "until the wrath pass over," which shall extinguish the antichrist, he shows that after the wrath the flesh shall go forth from the sepulchre, into which before the wrath it had been brought. For from storehouses nothing else is carried out than what is brought in; and after the rooting-out of the antichrist the resurrection shall be set in motion.

We know, moreover, that as by voices, so by things too, it was prophesied. As much by deeds as by words is the resurrection proclaimed: when Moses hides his hand in his bosom and brings it forth as dead, and again puts it in and draws it out alive — does this not portend concerning the whole man? — since the threefold power of God was denoted through those three signs: in its own order, first to subdue to man the devil, the serpent, though formidable; then to draw back the flesh from the bosom of death; and so to bring all blood to judgment. Concerning which, in the same prophet: "For your blood too," God says, "I will require of all the beasts, and of the hand of man and of the hand of his brother I will require it." Further, nothing is required except what is demanded back; nothing is demanded back except what shall also be rendered; and surely that shall be rendered which in the name of vengeance shall be demanded back and required. For that cannot be avenged which was not at all. But it shall be, while it is restored, that it may be avenged. So whatever is proclaimed upon the blood is directed unto the flesh, without which there will be no blood. The flesh shall be raised up, that the blood may be avenged. There are also some things so pronounced that they lack indeed the cloud of allegory, yet none the less thirst for the interpretation of their very simplicity — such as that in Isaiah: "I will kill, and I will make alive." Certainly after He has killed He will make alive. Therefore, killing through death, He will make alive through resurrection. But it is the flesh that is killed through death; the flesh, therefore, shall also be made alive through resurrection. Certainly if to kill is to snatch the soul from the flesh, to make alive — its contrary — is to bring the soul back to the flesh; the flesh must of necessity rise again, to which the soul, snatched away by killing, must be brought back by making-alive.

If, therefore, both allegorical Scriptures and the arguments of things and simple voices shed light upon the resurrection of the flesh — though without the naming of the substance itself — how much more shall those not be drawn into question which determine this hope upon the very bodily substances by special mention? Take Ezekiel. "And the hand of the Lord," he says, "was upon me, and the Lord brought me out in the spirit and set me in the midst of a field" — it was filled with bones — "and led me round about over them in a circuit, and behold, many upon the face of the field. And behold, very dry. And He said to me, Son of man, shall these bones live? And I said, Adonai, Lord, you know.
