And He said to me, Prophesy upon these bones, and you shall say, Dry bones, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord Adonai to these bones: Behold, I bring into you spirit, and you shall live; and I will give into you spirit, and I will bring back into you flesh; I will put skin about you, and will give into you spirit, and you shall live, and shall know that I am the Lord. And I prophesied according to the command, and behold a voice, while I prophesy, and behold a motion, and the bones came together, bone to bone. And I saw, and behold, upon the bones sinews and flesh came up, and flesh was set about them, and there was no spirit in them. And He said to me, Prophesy to the spirit, son of man, prophesy and say to the spirit, Thus says the Lord Adonai: From the four winds come, O spirit, and breathe upon these slain, and let them live. And I prophesied to the spirit as He commanded me, and the spirit entered into them, and they lived and stood upon their feet, an exceeding great host. And He said to me, Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel. They say, Our bones are dried up, and our hope has perished; we are torn away among them. Therefore prophesy to them: Behold, I open your sepulchres, and will bring you up out of your sepulchres, my people, and will lead you into the land of Israel; and you shall know that I am the Lord, that I have opened your sepulchres and brought you out of your sepulchres, my people; and I will give you spirit, and you shall live and shall rest in your own land; and you shall know that I the Lord have spoken and have done it, says the Lord."

This proclamation too I know how they shake into an allegorical argument: because by saying, "These bones are the whole house of Israel," He made them an image of Israel, and transferred them from their proper condition; and so it is a figured, not a true, proclamation of resurrection. For the state of the Jews is somehow figured as dead and dried up and dispersed over the field of the world. And so even the image of resurrection is allegorized upon it, because it must be gathered together again and joined again, bone to bone — that is, tribe to tribe and people to people — and re-embodied with the flesh of resources and the sinews of a kingdom; and so out of the sepulchres — that is, out of the most dismal and foul dwelling-places of captivity — be led forth, and breathe again under the name of refreshment, and live thenceforth in their own land of Judaea. And what after these things? They will die, without doubt. And what after death? No raising up, I suppose, if this be not the very thing that is revealed to Ezekiel. But indeed resurrection is proclaimed elsewhere too; therefore this also will be it, and they rashly turn it into the state of Jewish affairs. Or if that is another than the one we defend, it is nothing to me, provided there be both a resurrection of bodies, as also of Jewish affairs. In short, by this very thing, that the return of the Jewish state is figured by the re-embodying and re-uniting of bones, it is proved that this too shall befall the bones. For a figure could not be composed of bones, were not this very thing to befall the bones too. For although the moulding of the truth is in the image, the image itself is in the truth of itself. It must of necessity first be to itself that to which another is configured. From an empty thing no likeness fits; of a nothing no parable agrees. So it will be necessary to believe also a re-quickening and a re-breathing of bones, such as is said, from which can be expressed the reformation of Jewish affairs, such as is fashioned thereon. But it is more religious that the truth be defended from the authority of its own simplicity, which the sense of the divine proposition demands. For if this vision regarded Jewish affairs, immediately upon the situation of the bones being revealed He would have subjoined, "These bones are the whole house of Israel," and the rest in order. But when, the bones being shown, He says something concerning their own hope, Israel not yet named, and tries the faith of the prophet — "Son of man, shall these bones live?" — so that he too answers, "Lord, you know" — surely God would not have tried the faith of the prophet concerning a matter which was not to be, which Israel had never heard, which it ought not to be believed. But because the resurrection of the dead was indeed proclaimed, while Israel, distrusting through its incredulity, was scandalized, and looking at the aspect of an aging burial despaired of resurrection — or rather directed its mind not to it, but to its own circumstances — therefore God both prepared the prophet, who himself was likewise doubtful, for steadfastness of proclamation, the order of resurrection being revealed, and commanded the people to believe what He revealed to the prophet, saying that they themselves were the bones that were to rise again, who did not believe that they would rise again. In short, in the close: "And you shall know," He says, "that I the Lord have spoken and have done it" — about to do, surely, what He had spoken. But not about to do what He spoke, if about to do otherwise than He spoke.

Plainly, if the people too were murmuring allegorically about their dried-up bones and their lost hope, querulous at the issue of the dispersion, God would rightly seem to have consoled a figured despair with a figured promise. But since the injury of the dispersion had not yet befallen the people, while the hope of resurrection had very often fallen among them, and it is manifest that, shaken by the destruction of bodies, he was undermining their confidence in resurrection — so God too was rebuilding the faith which the people was destroying. And yet, even if Israel was then mourning under some conflict of present affairs, not on that account was the intention of the revelation to be taken as a parable, but as a testimony of resurrection — so that He might raise them into that hope, of eternal salvation, namely, and a more necessary restitution, and turn them from regard to present affairs. For to this end also the other prophets: "You shall go forth from the sepulchres, like calves loosed from bonds, and you shall tread down your enemies." And again: "Your heart shall rejoice, and your bones shall spring up like grass" — because grass too is reformed from the dissolution and corruption of seed. In sum, if the image of the rising bones is properly contended to be of the state of Israel, why is the same hope announced not to Israel only, but to all nations also — of the re-embodying and re-animating of the remnants, and of the dead to be roused up from the sepulchres? For it is said of all: "The dead shall live, and shall rise from the sepulchres; for the dew which is from You is healing to their bones." Likewise elsewhere: "All flesh shall come to adore in My sight, says the Lord." When? When the fashion of this world shall begin to pass away. For above: "As the new heaven and the new earth which I make abide in My sight, says the Lord, so shall your seed stand." Then, therefore, what He subjoins too shall be fulfilled: "And they shall go forth" — out of the sepulchres, surely — "and shall see the limbs of those who acted impiously, for their worm shall not die and their fire shall not be quenched; and they shall be a spectacle to all flesh" — that flesh, namely, which, raised up and gone forth from the sepulchres, shall adore the Lord for this grace.

But lest the resurrection seem proclaimed only of those bodies which are committed to sepulchres, you have it written: "And I will command the fishes of the sea, and they shall belch up the bones that are eaten, and I will make joint to joint and bone to bone." "Therefore," you say, "the fishes too shall be raised up, and the other beasts and the carnivorous birds, to vomit back those whom they have eaten — since in Moses too you read that blood is required of all the beasts?" Not at all. But beasts and fishes are named in the rendering-back of flesh and blood for this reason: that the resurrection even of devoured bodies may be the more expressed, since the exaction is decreed of the devourers themselves. I think, moreover, that a fit document of this divine power too is Jonah, when, uncorrupted in both substances, flesh and soul, he is unrolled from the belly of the fish. And surely the entrails of the whale would have sufficed for three days to digest the flesh, more than the coffin, more than the sepulchre, more than the age of some quiet and hidden burial — saving the fact that He figured both beasts (men savage especially toward the Christian name, or even the very angels of iniquity) of whom blood shall be exacted through a vengeance to be weighed out. Who, then, is more disposed to learning than to presumption, and more diligent in believing than in contending, and more religious toward the divine wisdom than wanton toward his own — who, hearing that anything is appointed by God upon flesh and skins and sinews and bones, will devise some other meaning of these, as though what is proclaimed upon these substances be not appointed upon man? For either nothing is appointed upon man — not the bounty of the kingdom, not the severity of judgment, not whatever the resurrection is — or, if it is appointed upon man, it must of necessity be appointed upon those substances of which man is built, upon whom it is appointed. This too I ask of those most subtle transmuters of bones and flesh and sinews and sepulchres: why, if at any time anything is pronounced upon the soul, they interpret the soul as nothing else, nor refashion it into an argument for another thing — but when anything is decreed upon some bodily form, they assert anything rather than what is named? If the bodily things are parables, then the soul-things too; if not the soul-things too, then neither the bodily. For man is body as much as soul; so that the one form cannot admit riddles, the other exclude them.

Enough of this from the prophetic instrument. Now I appeal to the Gospels — here too about to meet first that same cunning of theirs who likewise contend that the Lord pronounced everything in parables, because it is written: "All these things Jesus spoke in parables, and without a parable He did not speak to them" — to the Jews, namely. For the disciples too say, "Why do you speak in parables?" and the Lord, "Therefore I speak in parables to them, that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not hear," according to Isaiah. But if to the Jews in parables, then not to all; if not to all in parables, then not always nor all things parables, but certain things, when to certain men. To certain men, that is, while to the Jews; sometimes plainly even to the disciples. But consider how the Scripture reports it: "But He spoke also a parable to them." Therefore He also spoke what was not a parable; for it would not be noted, when He spoke a parable, if He always spoke so. And yet you will find no parable that is not either expounded by Himself — as that of the sower in the administration of the word — or pre-illumined by the commentator of the Gospel — as of the proud judge and the insistent widow, toward perseverance in prayer — or to be conjectured of one's own accord — as of the fig tree deferred in hope, after the likeness of Jewish unfruitfulness. But if not even parables overshadow the light of the Gospel, so far is it from being that sentences and definitions, whose nature is open, should taste otherwise than they sound. But by definitions and sentences the Lord decrees whether judgment or the kingdom of God or resurrection. "It shall be more tolerable," He says, "for Tyre and Sidon in the day of judgment"; and, "Tell them that the kingdom of God has drawn near"; and, "It shall be recompensed to you in the resurrection of the just." If the names are absolute of the things — that is, of judgment and the kingdom of God and resurrection — so that none of them can be compressed into a parable, neither let those things be forced into parables which are proclaimed concerning the disposition and the transaction and the suffering of the kingdom, the judgment, and the resurrection; and so the bodily things will be defended as appointed for bodily things — that is, not spiritual, because not figured. For on this account too we laid the foundation that the body of the soul, as much as that of the flesh, is liable to wages to be weighed out for the common operation — lest the corporeality of the soul, supplying an occasion of figures, exclude the corporeality of the flesh, when both must be believed partakers of the kingdom and the judgment and the resurrection. And now we proceed to this, that we may demonstrate the carnal corporeality properly to be signified by the Lord in every mention of resurrection — saving the soul-bound one, which too few have received.

First, when He says that He came to this end, that He might save what had perished, what do you say has perished? Man, without doubt. The whole, or in part? The whole, surely. Since transgression, which is the cause of human perdition, committed as much by the prompting of the soul out of concupiscence as by the act of the flesh out of tasting, has inscribed the whole man with the sentence of transgression, and thence has filled him with the deserved perdition. The whole, then, shall be made safe who perished wholly by sinning. Unless that sheep too is lost without a body and recalled without a body. For if its flesh too with its soul — which is the whole beast — is borne upon the shoulders of the good shepherd, surely it is an example of man to be restored out of both substances. Or how unworthy of God, to bring half a man unto salvation — almost to do less; when even among secular princes a full indulgence is always claimed! Is the devil understood the stronger for man's injury, dashing the whole of him down — while God shall be reported the weaker, not revealing the whole of him? But on the other hand the apostle too suggests, "Where offence has abounded, there grace has superabounded." How, in short, shall he be held safe who can also be called lost? — lost in flesh, namely, but safe in soul. Unless that even the soul be of necessity set in the perished, that it may be able to be made safe; for that ought to be made safe which has been lost. But further, we receive the immortality of the soul, so that, when lost, it is believed not unto destruction, but unto punishment, that is, unto hell. And if so, salvation will now look not to the soul — safe, namely, by its own nature through immortality — but to the flesh rather, which all agree to be perishable. Or if the soul too is perishable — that is, not immortal, like the flesh — then to the flesh too that form must equally avail, being likewise mortal and perishable, because the Lord is about to save what perishes. I do not now wish, with a contentious rope, to draw man this way or that, according as perdition demands him, since salvation from both sides appoints him, made equal in both substances. For behold, of whichever substance you presume man to have perished, of the other he does not perish. Safe, then, he will already be of that of which he does not perish, and none the less shall be made safe of that of which he perishes. You have the restitution of the whole man, while both whatever of him perishes the Lord is about to make safe, and whatever does not perish He surely will not let perish. Who further will doubt of the security of either substance, when the one is to attain salvation, the other is not to lose it? And yet the Lord still expresses the sense of the matter, saying, "I came not to do My own will, but the will of the Father who sent Me." What, I ask you? "That of all that He gave Me I should lose nothing, but should raise it up in the last day." What had Christ received from the Father, except that which He had also put on? Man, without doubt, the texture of flesh and soul. Neither, then, of those things which He received will He suffer to perish — nay, not anything of either, nay, not even a little. But if a little is the flesh, then not the flesh either, because not a little, nor anything, because not anything. But on the other hand, if He shall not raise up the flesh too in the last day, then He suffers no little of man to perish, but — for so great a part, I should say — nearly the whole. Pressing further, "This is the will of the Father, that everyone who beholds the Son and believes in Him should have eternal life, and I should raise him up in the last day" — He builds the fullness of resurrection. For He distributes to each substance, through its offices, the proper wage of salvation: both to the flesh, through which the Son was beheld, and to the soul, through which He was believed. "Then," you will say, "the thing will be promised to those by whom Christ was seen." Be it plainly so, provided that the same hope flowed thence to us also. For if to those who saw, and therefore believed, the works of flesh and soul were then fruitful, much more to us. For "happier," He says, "are those who have not seen and believe" — since, even were the resurrection of the flesh denied to those, surely it would have fitted the happier. For how happy, if they are to perish in part?

But He also commands that He rather be feared who kills body and soul in hell — that is, the Lord alone — not those who kill the body, but can do nothing to the soul — that is, human powers. So far is the soul here recognized as immortal by nature, which cannot be killed by men, and the flesh as having mortality, whose is the killing; and so too the resurrection of the dead is of the flesh, which, unless raised up, cannot be killed in hell. But since here too a quibble is raised over the interpretation of "body," I will understand the body of man as nothing else than all that mass of flesh, by whatever kind of matters it is fitted and varied, which is seen, which is held, which finally is killed by men. So too I will admit the body of a wall to be nothing else than the masonry, the stones, the bricks. If anyone brings in some hidden body, let him show, reveal, prove it to be also that which is killed by man, and of that it will have been said. Likewise if the body of the soul is opposed, the cunning will be idle. For when both are proposed — body and soul killed in hell — the body is distinguished from the soul, and it is left to understand the body to be that which is at hand, the flesh, namely, which, just as it shall be killed in hell, if it has not rather feared to be killed by God, so shall it also be made alive unto eternal life, if it has preferred rather to be slain by men. Likewise if anyone shall snatch the killing of flesh and soul in hell as unto the destruction and end of both substances, not unto punishment (as though to be consumed, not to be punished), let him recall that the fire of hell is proclaimed eternal unto eternal penalty, and thence recognize the eternity of the killing, which therefore is to be more feared than the human and temporal one. Then too he will believe substances eternal whose killing unto penalty is eternal. Certainly, since after the resurrection the body with the soul is to be killed by God in hell, it will be sufficiently established concerning both — both the carnal resurrection and the eternal killing. Most absurd, otherwise, if the flesh be on this account raised up to be killed in hell, that it may be ended — which not even unraised it would suffer. For this, namely, it would be remade: that there be no one to whom not-being has now befallen! Propping us upon the same hope, He subjoins also the example of the sparrows: that of two not one shall fall to the ground without the will of God — that you may believe that the flesh too, which has fallen to the ground, can likewise rise again through the will of the same God. For although this is not granted to sparrows, yet we are of more worth than many sparrows, in that, falling, we rise again — affirming that the very hairs of whose head are all numbered, surely He promises in turn to be safe. For what reason would have reduced to number things about to perish — unless because this is the meaning: "That of all that the Father gave Me I should lose nothing," that is, not a hair, just as not an eye nor a tooth? For whence shall there be weeping and gnashing of teeth, except from eyes and from teeth? — the body, namely, killed too in hell and thrust into the outer darkness, which are the proper torments of the eyes; if anyone has been clothed at the wedding with works less worthy, to be bound at once hand and foot, as one who has risen with a body. So therefore his reclining too in the kingdom of God, and sitting on the thrones of Christ, and standing then at the right hand or the left, and eating of the tree of life, are most faithful tokens of a bodily disposition.

Let us now see whether, dashing down also the craft of the Sadducees, He has not the more set up our view. The cause, I think, of the question was the destruction of the resurrection — since the Sadducees admit the salvation neither of the soul nor of the flesh — and therefore from that very form of resurrection by which faith is most undermined they fitted an argument to their problem: under the pretext, namely, of the flesh's marrying or not after the resurrection, under the person of that woman who, married to seven brothers, was held in doubt to which of them she should be restored. Now let the senses both of the question and of the answer be kept, and the controversy is met. For if the Sadducees indeed spurned the resurrection, while the Lord confirmed it — both rebuking them as ignorant of the Scriptures, namely those which had proclaimed the resurrection, and as incredulous of the power of God, fit surely for raising up the dead — at last subjoining, "But that the dead rise" — without doubt, by confirming that there is that which was denied, that is, the resurrection of the dead with God of the living, He confirmed it also to be such as was denied, of both human substances, namely. For if He then denied that they would marry, He did not therefore demonstrate that they would not rise either. Rather He called them sons of the resurrection, having somehow to be born through it; after which they shall not marry, but, being raised up — "For they shall be like the angels" — in that they shall not marry, because they shall not die; but in that they shall pass over into the angelic state, through that garment of incorruptibility, yet through a transmutation of the raised-up substance. For the rest, it would not even be asked whether we should be married or about to die again or not, were not the restitution most especially called into doubt of that substance which properly is occupied with both death and marriage, that is, the flesh. You have, therefore, the Lord confirming against the heretics of the Jews — what is even now denied among the Sadducees of the Christians — a solid resurrection.

So too, if He says that the flesh profits nothing, the sense must be directed from the matter of the saying. For because they thought His word hard and intolerable — as though He had determined that His flesh was truly to be eaten by them — that He might dispose the state of salvation into the spirit, He premised, "It is the spirit that quickens," and so subjoined, "The flesh profits nothing" — for quickening, namely. He follows out also what He would have understood by spirit: "The words which I have spoken to you are spirit, are life." As also above: "He who hears My words, and believes Him who sent Me, has eternal life, and shall not come into judgment, but shall pass from death to life." And so, constituting the word the quickener — because the word is spirit and life — He also called the same His flesh, because the word too had been made flesh, and therefore was to be sought after unto the cause of life, and devoured by hearing, and ruminated by understanding, and digested by faith. For a little before He had also pronounced His flesh to be the heavenly bread too, urging everywhere through allegory the memory of the necessary foods of the fathers, who had preferred the bread and flesh of the Egyptians to the divine calling. Therefore, turned to their reconsiderings — because He had perceived that they were to be scattered — "The flesh," He says, "profits nothing." What is this to the destruction of the flesh's resurrection? — as though it may not be that there is something which, though it profit nothing itself, yet something else can profit it? The spirit profits; for it quickens. The flesh profits nothing; for it is mortified. And so, according to us, He rather set down the proposition of both. For showing what profits and what profits not, He at once illumined what profits which — the spirit, namely, quickener of the mortified flesh. "For the hour shall come," He says, "when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear shall live." What is dead, but the flesh? and what is the voice of God, but the word? and what is the word, but the spirit — rightly about to raise up the flesh, which it was made itself, and out of the death which it suffered itself, and out of the sepulchre into which it was brought itself? In short, when He says, "Marvel not, for the hour shall come in which all who are in the monuments shall hear the voice of the Son of God, and shall come forth — those who did good, unto the resurrection of life; those who did evil, unto the resurrection of judgment" — no one can any longer interpret the dead who are in the monuments as other than bodies and flesh; because the monuments themselves are nothing else than the stables of corpses, since even those very men of old — that is, sinners, that is, dead through ignorance of God, whom the heretics argue to be understood as the monuments — are openly proclaimed to be about to come forth from the monuments unto judgment. But how shall monuments come forth from monuments?

After the sayings of the Lord, what shall we believe His deeds too mean — His raising the dead from coffins, from sepulchres? To what end is this? If to a simple display of power, or to a present grace of re-animation, it is no such great thing for Him to raise up those about to die again. But indeed, if rather to set apart faith in a future resurrection, then that one too is prescribed as bodily, from the form of His own document. Nor will I endure those who say that the resurrection, then appointed for the soul alone, ran forward into the flesh too because the resurrection of the invisible soul could not otherwise be shown than through the raising up of a visible substance. They know God ill who think He cannot do what they do not think; and yet they know He could, if they know the instrument of John. For He who set before the sight souls as yet alone, of the martyrs, resting under the altar, could surely also have shown them rising again to the eyes without flesh. But I prefer that God cannot deceive — weak only in falsehood — lest He seem to have premised documents otherwise than He disposed the matter; nay rather, lest, if He could not bring in an example of resurrection without flesh, much more He could not exhibit the fullness of the example in the same substance. But no example is greater than that of which it is an example. But it is greater, if souls shall be raised up with the body unto a document of rising again without the body — so that the whole salvation of man should patronize the half — when the condition of examples would rather require that which was the less held, the resurrection, I mean, of the soul alone, as a taste of the flesh too about to rise again in its own time. And indeed, according to our true estimation, those examples of the dead raised up by the Lord did indeed commend the resurrection of both flesh and soul, lest this gift be denied to either substance; yet, in so far as they were examples, they set forth something the less (for they were raised up not unto glory nor unto incorruptibility, but unto another death) than Christ set forth.

The apostolic instruments too attest the resurrection. For the apostles too had no other business — at least among Israel — than of unsealing the old testament and sealing the new, and rather now of preaching God in Christ. So too concerning resurrection they brought in nothing new, except that they announced it too unto the glory of Christ — for the rest, received by a simple and now known faith, without any question of its quality, the Sadducees alone gainsaying. So far was it easier to deny the resurrection of the dead altogether than to understand it otherwise. You have Paul before the high priests, under the tribune, among the Sadducees and Pharisees, a professor of his faith. "Men, brethren," he says, "I am a Pharisee, the son of Pharisees; concerning the hope and the resurrection I am now judged before you" — the common one, surely — lest, because he now seemed a transgressor of the law, he be thought to side with the Sadducees on the chief article of the whole faith, that is, on the resurrection. So, what he did not wish to seem to rescind, he surely confirmed — the faith of resurrection, according to the Pharisees — spurning its deniers, the Sadducees. Likewise before Agrippa he says that he brings forward nothing beyond what the prophets had announced. Therefore he kept the resurrection too such as the prophets had announced. For commemorating that concerning the resurrection of the dead it is written in Moses, he knew it bodily, in which, namely, the blood of man shall have to be required. And so he proclaimed it such as both the Pharisees had received and the Lord Himself had defended, and such as the Sadducees, lest they believe it such too, had wished not to be at all. But neither had the Athenians understood any other to be portended by Paul. In short, they mocked — about to mock not at all, if they had heard from him the restitution of the soul alone; for they would have received the more frequent presumption of their own native philosophy. But when the proclamation of a resurrection unheard of before struck the nations by its very novelty, and a worthy incredulity began to torture faith with questions concerning so great a matter, then the apostle too, through almost the whole instrument, took care to corroborate faith in this hope — both showing that it is, and not yet transacted; and — what was the more asked — bodily; and — what was moreover doubted — not bodily otherwise.

But it is no wonder if arguments are caught even from his own instrument, since "there must be heresies" — which could not be, if the Scriptures could not also be understood perversely. In short, the heresies, having lit upon two men set forth by the apostle — the inner, that is, the soul, and the outer, that is, the flesh — have adjudged salvation indeed to the soul, that is, the inner man, but destruction to the flesh, that is, the outer; because it is written to the Corinthians: "For although our outer man is corrupted, yet the inner is renewed day by day." Now neither is the soul of itself man, which was inserted afterward into the moulding already called man, nor is the flesh man without the soul, which after the exile of the soul is inscribed a corpse. So the word "man" is, as it were, a clasp of the two joined substances, under which word they cannot exist except as cohering. Further, the apostle prefers that the inner man be understood not so much the soul as the mind and the disposition — that is, not the substance itself, but the savour of the substance. Since, writing to the Ephesians that Christ dwells in the inner man, he signified the Lord to be intimated, surely, to the senses. In short, he added: "By faith, and in your hearts, and in love" — setting down faith and love not as substantives of the soul, but as conceptives; but saying "in your hearts," which are substantives of the flesh, he has now reckoned even the inner man himself to the flesh, whom he constituted in the heart. Look now how he has alleged that the outer man indeed is corrupted, but the inner is renewed day by day. Do not affirm that corruption of the flesh which it suffers from the day of death in perpetuity henceforth; but that which in the span of this life, before death and up to death, it experiences through vexations and pressures, torments and punishments, for the cause of the Name. For here too the inner man shall have to be renewed by the suggestion of the spirit, advancing in faith and discipline day by day — not there, that is, not after the resurrection, where surely we shall not be renewed day by day, but once for all, to the sum. Learn from what follows: "For that which is at present," he says, "temporal and light of our pressure, by a surpassing into a surpassing, shall accomplish for us an eternal weight of glory — we looking not at the things which are seen" — that is, sufferings — "but at the things which are not seen" — that is, the wages. "For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal." For the pressures and injuries by which the outer man is corrupted, he affirms to be on that account contemptible, as light and temporal — preferring the weight of eternal, invisible wages and glory, in compensation of the labours by which here the flesh is corrupted by suffering. So far is that not the corruption which they ascribe to the outer man as the perpetual destruction of the flesh, to drive out resurrection. So too elsewhere: "Since," he says, "we suffer together, that we may also be glorified together: for I reckon that the sufferings of this time are not worthy of the future glory which is to be revealed in us." And here he shows the lesser troubles by their wages. Further, if through the flesh we suffer together — whose it properly is to be corrupted by sufferings — to the same will belong also what is promised for the suffering-together. And indeed, about to ascribe to the flesh the propriety of pressures, as above, he says, "But when we came into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest"; then, that he might give the soul too a suffering-together, "In all things," he says, "we were pressed — without, fightings" — warring down the flesh, namely — "within, fear" — afflicting the soul, namely. So far, even if the outer man is corrupted, it shall be understood corrupted not as losing resurrection, but as enduring vexation, and from this not without the inner. So it will belong to both to be glorified together too, as also to suffer together. According to the colleges of labours, the consortia of wages too must of necessity run their course.

He pursues the same view still further, preferring rewards to vexations. "For we know," he says, "that even if the earthly house of this our tabernacle be dissolved, we have a house not made with hands, eternal, in the heavens" — that is, through this, that our flesh shall be dissolved through sufferings, we are to attain a dwelling in the heavens. He had remembered the evangelic definition: "Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Yet he did not deny the restitution of the flesh, if he set against it the compensation of a wage — since the compensation is owed to that very thing to which the dissolution is reckoned, namely the flesh. But because he had called the flesh a house, he wished elegantly, even in the comparison of the wage, to use the word "house" — promising to the very house which shall be dissolved through suffering a better house through resurrection (for the Lord too promises many mansions, as it were houses, with the Father; although it can be understood also of the dwelling of the world, which being dissolved, an eternal seat is promised in the heavens, because the things which follow, manifestly pertaining to the flesh, show that the former do not pertain to the flesh): for the apostle makes a division when he subjoins, "For in this too we groan, desiring to be clothed over with our dwelling which is from heaven, if so be that, unclothed, we be not found naked" — that is, we wish to be clothed over with the heavenly virtue of eternity before we are unclothed of the flesh. For the privilege of this grace awaits those who at the coming of the Lord shall be caught in the flesh, and on account of the hardships of the times of the antichrist shall deserve, by the compendium of a death discharged through transmutation, to run together with those who rise — as he writes to the Thessalonians: "For this we say to you in the word of the Lord, that we who live, who remain unto the coming of the Lord, shall not anticipate those who have slept; for the Lord Himself, at the command and at the voice of the archangel and at the trumpet of God, shall descend from heaven, and the dead in Christ shall rise first; then we, together with them, shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air; and so shall we ever be with the Lord."

The transmutation of these he renders to the Corinthians, saying, "We shall all indeed rise again, but we shall not all be transmuted, in an atom, in a momentary motion of the eye, at the last trumpet" — but those alone, namely, who shall be found in the flesh. "And the dead," he says, "shall rise, we shall be transmuted." With this disposition, then, first foreseen, you will recall the rest to the higher sense. For when he adds, "For this corruptive must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality" — this will be that dwelling from heaven which, groaning in this flesh, we desire to be clothed over with — surely over the flesh in which we shall be caught; because he says that we are burdened, who are in the tabernacle, which we would not be unclothed of, but rather clothed over, that the mortal may be devoured by life — that is, while we are transmuted, by clothing over with that which is of the heavens. For who would not desire, while he is in the flesh, to be clothed over with immortality and to continue life, death being made gain through a substitutionary transmutation, that he experience not hell, which would exact even to the last farthing? For the rest, even after the resurrection he is to attain transmutation, having now experienced hell. For hence we define that the flesh shall in every way rise again, and that from that transmutation it shall, supervening, take up the angelic state. Or, if in those alone who shall be found in the flesh it must be transmuted, that the mortal may be devoured by life — that is, the flesh by that heavenly and eternal over-garment — then those who shall be caught dead will not attain life, being deprived now of the material and, so to speak, the food of life, that is, the flesh; or it is necessary that they too receive it, that in them too the mortal may be devoured by life, if they are to attain life. "But in the dead," you say, "this mortal will already have been devoured." Not in all, surely. For how many may be found even but a day old — corpses so recent that nothing in them can seem devoured? For surely you reckon "devoured" as nothing else than intercepted, abolished, snatched from every sense, ceasing in every kind to appear. But neither will it be established that the most ancient corpses of the Giants are devoured, whose frames yet live. We have already spoken of this elsewhere. But also lately in this city, when the sacrilegious foundations of the odeon were being laid upon so many old burials, the people shuddered at bones of nearly five hundred years still moist and at hairs still smelling. It is agreed that not only bones endure, but even teeth last incorrupt — which are retained as it were seeds of the body about to sprout in the resurrection. Finally, even if then the mortal be found devoured in all the dead — surely by death, surely by age, surely through time — yet is it by life, is it by the over-garment, is it by the in-pouring of immortality? Further, he who says that the mortal shall be devoured by these, has denied it of those. And surely it will be fitting that this be accomplished and afforded by the divine powers, not by natural laws. Therefore, since that which is mortal is to be devoured by life, it must in every way be exhibited, that it may be devoured, and devoured that it may be transmuted. If you should say that fire must be kindled, you cannot affirm that by which it is kindled to be necessary in one place, not in another. So too when he infulces, "If so be that, unclothed, we be not found naked" — concerning those, namely, who shall not be caught in life nor in the flesh by the day of the Lord — he denied that those whom he foretold as unclothed should be otherwise naked, except that he wished them understood as reclothed with the same substance of which they had been spoiled. For as naked they shall be found, the flesh laid down, or in part torn off or worn away (for this too may be called nakedness); thereafter they shall receive it, that, reclothed with flesh, they may be able to become also clothed over with immortality; for to be clothed over cannot be fitting except to one already clothed.

Likewise when he says, "And so, confident always, and knowing that, while we dwell in the body, we are away from the Lord — for we walk by faith, not by sight" — it is manifest that this too does not pertain to the darkening of the flesh, as though separating us from the Lord. For here too an exhortation to disdain this life is set forth, since we are away from the Lord so long as we live, walking by faith, not by sight — that is, by hope, not by reality. And therefore he subjoins, "But being confident, and accounting it good rather to be away from the body and to dwell with the Lord" — that is, that we may walk rather by sight than by faith, by reality rather than by hope. You see how here too he refers the contempt of bodies to the excellence of martyrdoms. For no one, away from the body, dwells at once with the Lord, except by the prerogative of martyrdom, being about to lodge in paradise, namely, not in hell. But had words failed the apostle for signifying departure from the body? Or does he by design speak even with novelty? For, wishing to signify a temporal absence from the body, he said that we are away from it, since he who is away will also return into his dwelling. Thence too, to all: "And therefore we strive," he says, "whether away or dwelling, to be pleasing to God; for we must all be made manifest before the tribunal of Christ Jesus." If all, then also wholly; if wholly, then both the inner and the outer, that is, both souls and bodies: "that each one," he says, "may carry back the things done through the body, according as he has done, good or evil." How now you should read this, I ask. For he has built it, as it were confusedly, by hyperbaton. Whether the things to be carried back through the body, or the things done through the body? But even if the things to be carried back are through the body, the resurrection is undoubtedly bodily; and if the things done are through the body, surely they must be weighed out through the body, through which also they were done. So this whole treatment of the apostle from the head, woven down to such a close — by which the resurrection of the flesh is shown — shall be understood according to those things which consort with the close.

For if you look back still further, whence the mention of the outer and inner man was brought in, will you not find both the dignity and the hope of the flesh entire? For when, concerning the light which God has shone in our hearts unto the illumination of the recognition of His glory in the person of Christ, he says that we have this treasure in earthen vessels — that is, in the flesh — shall it be destroyed because it is earthen according to its origin in slime, or exalted because it is the storehouse of a divine treasure? But on the other hand, if the very light of God, that true one which is in the person of Christ, contains life in itself, and that life is committed with the light into the flesh — is that to perish into which life is committed? Plainly thus the treasure too is to perish; for perishable things are committed to perishable things, as new wine to old skins. When likewise he subjoins, "Always carrying about the mortification of Christ Jesus in our body" — what kind of thing is that which, after the temple of God, can now be called also the sepulchre of Christ? But why do we carry about the mortification of the Lord in the body? "That the life too," he says, "may be manifested." Where? In the body. In what kind? In the mortal. Therefore in the flesh, plainly mortal according to fault, but also vital according to grace — see how great, that in it the life of Christ may be manifested! In a thing, then, foreign to salvation, in a substance of perpetual dissolution, shall the eternal, perennial, incorrupt — now even the divine — life of Christ be manifested? Or of what time shall the life of the Lord be manifested in our body? That, indeed, which He lived up to the passion, which was not only in the open among the Jews, but is now also published to all nations? So far does he signify that life which broke the adamantine gates of death and the brazen bars of hell, which thenceforth is now ours. In short, it shall be manifested in the body. When? After death. How? While we rise again in the body, as Christ too. For lest anyone argue that the life of Jesus has now to be manifested in our body through the discipline of sanctity and patience and righteousness and wisdom, by which the life of the Lord flourished, the most provident intention of the apostle presses in: "For if we who live are delivered unto death for Jesus' sake, that the life of Him may be manifested in our mortal body." So far does he say that this shall be in our body when we are dead. But if then, how, except by its being raised up? Likewise too in the close: "Knowing," he says, "that He who raised up Jesus will raise us up too with Him, because He has already risen from the dead." Except that "with Him" tastes of "as Him"; but if "as Him," surely not without flesh.

But again, by another blindness, they stumble upon two men — the old and the new — the apostle admonishing us to lay aside the old man, who is corrupted through the concupiscence of seduction, and to be renewed in the spirit of our disposition, and to put on the new man, who is created according to God in righteousness and the religion of truth — so that here too, by distinguishing into two substances — oldness to the flesh, newness to the soul — he may defend a perpetual corruption to the old, that is, the flesh. Further, if according to substances, neither is the soul a new man because later, nor the flesh therefore old because earlier. For how little time between the hand of God and the breath? I would dare to say: even if the soul be much earlier than the flesh, by this very thing, that the soul awaited to be filled, it made the flesh the earlier. For every consummation and perfection, even though in order it comes last, yet in effect it anticipates. That is rather the first without which the former cannot be. If the flesh is the old man, when is this? From the beginning? But Adam was wholly new, and out of the new no one was old. For even thenceforward, from the blessing of generation, flesh and soul come into being together, without a reckoning of time, as being sown together even in the womb — which we have taught in the commentary on the soul. They are tempered together in conception, are coeval in birth. These two men, indeed, of a double substance, yet not of differing age, so produce one man, while neither is the earlier. It is more correct that we be wholly either old or new; for by what means one of us could be the other we do not know. But the apostle manifestly marks the old man. For "Put off," he says, "according to the former conversation, the old man" — not according to the senility of any substance. For he does not bid us put off the flesh, but those things which elsewhere too he shows to be carnal — accusing works, not bodies — concerning which here too he subjoins, "Putting off lying, speak truth each one to his neighbour, for we are members one of another. Be angry, and sin not. Let not the sun go down upon your wrath. Neither give place to the devil. Let him who stole steal no more, but rather labour, working with his hands, that he may have to impart to him who is in need. Let no foul speech proceed out of your mouth, but such as is best for the edification of faith, that it may give grace to the hearers. And grieve not the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you are sealed unto the day of redemption. Let all bitterness and wrath and clamour and blasphemy and indignation be taken away from you, with all malice. But be kind one to another, merciful, forgiving one another, as God too forgave you in Christ." Therefore those who reckon the flesh the old man — why do they not hasten death for themselves, that, the old man laid aside, they may meet the precepts of the apostle? But we, who have believed that the whole faith is to be administered in the flesh — nay, even through the flesh, whose is both the mouth for uttering each best word, and the tongue for not blaspheming, and the heart for not being indignant, and the hand for working and bestowing — we defend that both the oldness of man and the newness pertain to a moral, not a substantial, difference. And so we likewise recognize the man who shall have been old according to the former conversation, the same to be said corrupted according to the concupiscence of seduction, just as old according to the former conversation, not according to the flesh, through perpetual destruction. For the rest, as safe in flesh as the same — having put off, namely, a vicious discipline, not a corpulence.

Such everywhere you may recognize the apostle, so condemning the works of the flesh that he seems to condemn the flesh — yet, lest anyone so think, providing it from the suggestion of other or cohering senses. For even when he says that those who are in the flesh cannot please God, he at once recalls from a depraved understanding to a sound one, adding, "But you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit." For those who, it was agreed, were in the flesh, by denying them to be in the flesh, he showed to be not in the works of the flesh; and so that those alone cannot please God, not who were in the flesh, but who lived carnally — but that those please God who, set in the flesh, walked according to the spirit. And again he says that the body indeed is dead, but on account of delinquency, just as the spirit is life on account of righteousness. But opposing life to death set in the flesh, without doubt he promised life too out of righteousness there where he determined death out of delinquency. For the rest, in vain did he oppose life to death, if it is not there where is also that to which he opposed it, surely to be excluded from the body. Further, if life excludes death from the body, it cannot accomplish this except it penetrate thither where is that which it excludes. And why do I speak more knottily, when the apostle speaks more absolutely? "For if," he says, "the spirit of Him who raised up Jesus dwells in you, He who raised up Jesus from the dead will raise up also your mortal bodies, on account of His spirit dwelling in you" — so that, even if anyone presume the soul to be the mortal body, since with this he cannot deny the flesh too, he be forced to acknowledge the resurrection of the flesh also, according to the communion of the same state. From what follows you may further learn that the works of the flesh are condemned, not the flesh itself. "And so, brethren," he says, "we are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh; for if you live according to the flesh, you shall die; but if by the spirit you mortify the acts of the flesh, you shall live." Now, to answer each point: if to those set in the flesh, yet living according to the spirit, salvation is promised, then the flesh is not contrary to salvation, but the operation of the flesh. But the operation of the flesh excluded — which is the cause of death — the flesh is now shown safe, lacking the cause of death. "For the law," he says, "of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus has manumitted me from the law of delinquency and of death" — surely from that which he premised to dwell in our members. Therefore now our members shall not be held by the law of death, because not by that of delinquency, from which they are manumitted. "For what was invalid in the law, in which it was weakened through the flesh, God, having sent His Son in the likeness of delinquent flesh, and through delinquency condemned delinquency in the flesh" — not the flesh in delinquency; for neither is the house condemned with its dweller. For he said that sin dwells in our body. But, delinquency condemned, the flesh is acquitted, just as, uncondemned, it was bound by that law of death and delinquency. So too he called the disposition of the flesh death, then also enmity toward God — but not the flesh itself. "To whom, then," you will say, "shall the disposition of the flesh be reckoned, if not to the substance itself?" Plainly, if you shall have proved that the flesh tastes anything of its own. But if without the soul there is no sense of anything, understand the disposition of the flesh to be referred to the soul, sometimes reckoned to the flesh, because it is administered on account of the flesh and through the flesh. And therefore he says that delinquency dwells in the flesh, because the soul too, by which delinquency is brought in, is a tenant of the flesh — mortified indeed, but not in its own, but in delinquency's name. For elsewhere too: "How," he says, "do you, as though living in the world, even now pass sentence?" — writing not to the dead, but to those who ought to cease living worldly.

For this will be the worldly life which he says is the old man crucified with Christ — not the corporeality, but the morality. For the rest, if we do not so take it, our corporeality is not crucified, nor has our flesh suffered the cross of Christ; but, as he added, "That the body of delinquency may be made void" — through the amendment of life, not through the destruction of the substance, as he says, "That hereafter we serve not delinquency." And so, that on this reckoning we who have died together with Christ may believe that we shall also live together with Him. "For so," he says, "do you too reckon yourselves indeed dead." To what? to the flesh? No, but to delinquency. Therefore they shall be safe to the flesh, but living to God in Christ Jesus — through the flesh, surely, to which they shall not be dead — dead to delinquency, namely, not to the flesh. For he further presses in: "Let not, then, delinquency reign in your mortal body, to obey it, and to exhibit your members as weapons of unrighteousness unto delinquency; but exhibit yourselves to God as living from the dead" — not as living, but as living from the dead — "and your members as weapons of righteousness." And again: "As you have exhibited your members servants to uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, so now too exhibit your members servants to righteousness unto sanctification; for when you were servants of delinquency, you were free of righteousness. What fruit, then, had you in those things of which you are now ashamed? for their end is death. But now, made free from delinquency, and made servants to God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end eternal life. For the wages of delinquency is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord." So through this whole series of senses, tearing our members away from injustice and delinquency and joining them to righteousness and holiness, and transferring the same from the wages of death to the gift of eternal life, he surely promises to the flesh the compensation of salvation — to which it would have fitted not at all that a proper discipline of holiness and righteousness be enjoined, were not the reward of the discipline also its own; nor would baptism itself be committed, if through regeneration it were not also inaugurated unto restitution — this too the apostle pressing in: "Or do you not know that whoever of us were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death? We were buried, then, with Him through baptism into death, that, as Christ rose from the dead, so we too may walk in newness of life." And lest you think it said of that life only which from faith through baptism is to be walked in newness, most providently he builds on: "For if we have been planted together with the likeness of the death of Christ, so shall we be also of His resurrection." For through the likeness we die in baptism, but through the truth we rise in the flesh, as Christ too — "That, as delinquency reigned in death, so grace too may reign through righteousness unto eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord." How so, if not equally in the flesh? For where there is death, there too is life after death, because there too is life before, where afterward death. For if the reign of death works nothing but the dissolution of the flesh, accordingly life, contrary to death, must work the contrary — that is, the reintegration of the flesh — that, as death had devoured by prevailing, so too the mortal devoured by immortality may be able to hear, "Where, O death, is your sting? where, O death, is your contention?" For so too grace shall there superabound where iniquity too abounded. So too shall virtue be perfected in weakness — saving what perished, quickening what is dead, healing what is stricken, doctoring what languished, redeeming what was snatched away, freeing what was enslaved, recalling what was seduced, raising up what was dashed down; and indeed from earth into heaven, where the Philippians too learn from the apostle our citizenship is, whence too we await our Saviour Jesus Christ, who shall transfigure the body of our humility, conformable to the body of His glory — without doubt after the resurrection, since not even Christ Himself was glorified before His passion. These shall be our bodies, which he beseeches the Romans to exhibit a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God. How living, if they are to perish? how holy, if they are profane? how pleasing, if they are condemned? Come now — what to the Thessalonians I should think written by the very ray of the sun, so clearly does it shine — how shall these light-shunners of the Scriptures take it? "But may the God of peace Himself sanctify you wholly." Is it not enough? But there follows: "And may your whole body and soul and spirit be preserved without complaint in the presence of the Lord." You have the whole substance of man appointed unto salvation, and at no other time than at the coming of the Lord, which is the key of the resurrection.

"But flesh," you say, "and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God by inheritance." We know this too is written, but of set purpose we deferred it until now — so that what the adversaries set up as a barrier in the very first line of battle, we might lay low in the last encounter, all their questions, as it were its auxiliaries, first cast down. But even now the preceding things will demand to be recognized, so that to this sense too its own origin may make a prejudgment. The apostle, I think, having disposed to the Corinthians with every distinction of ecclesiastical discipline, had concluded the sum both of his Gospel and of their faith in the commendation of the Lord's death and resurrection, that he might draw from there the rule of our hope too, whence it might stand firm. And so he subjoins: "But if Christ is preached, that He rose from the dead, how do some among you say there is no resurrection of the dead? which if there is not, neither has Christ risen. But if Christ has not risen, vain is our preaching, empty too is your faith. We are even found false witnesses of God, who have given testimony that He raised up Christ, whom He did not raise up. For if the dead rise not, neither has Christ risen. If Christ has not risen, vain is your faith, because you are yet in your sins, and those who have slept in Christ have perished." By these things, to the believing of what matter does he seem to build us up? To the resurrection, you say, of the dead, which was being denied — surely wishing it to be believed by His own example, the Lord's resurrection. Surely, you say. But is an example composed of diversity or of parity? Of parity, surely, you say. But how did Christ rise? in the flesh, or not? Without doubt, if you hear that He died, that He was buried, according to the Scriptures, not otherwise than in the flesh; equally you grant Him raised up in the flesh. For that very thing which fell in death, which lay in burial, the same too rose again — not so much Christ in the flesh as the flesh in Christ. Therefore, if to the example of Christ we shall rise, who rose in the flesh, then we shall not rise to the example of Christ, if we too rise not in the flesh. "Because through man," he says, "came death, and through man the resurrection" — so that he separated indeed the authors, of death Adam, of resurrection Christ, but constituted the resurrection of the same substance as the death, through the comparison of the authors themselves under the name of man. For "if, as in Adam all die, so too in Christ all shall be made alive" — in the flesh shall they be made alive in Christ, as in Adam they die in the flesh. "But each in his own order" — namely, because also in his own body. For the order of merits shall be disposed under the name of things disposed. But since merits are ascribed also to the body, the order of bodies too must of necessity be disposed, that there may be an order of merits. "But if some are even baptized for the dead" — we shall see whether reasonably. Surely he contends that they instituted this from that presumption by which others too thought a vicarious baptism would profit the flesh unto the hope of resurrection — which, unless bodily, would not otherwise be so bound by a bodily baptism. Why does he say that they too are baptized, if the bodies which are baptized do not rise? For the soul is sanctified not by washing, but by response. "Why are we too," he says, "in peril every hour?" — through the flesh, surely. "I die daily" — surely by the perils of the flesh, through which he even fought with beasts at Ephesus — those beasts, namely, of the Asiatic pressure, concerning which in the second to the same: "For we would not have you ignorant, brethren, of our pressure in Asia, that we were burdened beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we doubted of life." All these things, unless I am deceived, he enumerates to this end: that, unwilling that the flesh's conflict be believed vain, he wishes the flesh's resurrection to be believed beyond doubt. For the conflict of that must be held vain whose resurrection will be none. But someone will say: "How do the dead rise? and with what body do they come?" Now here he discusses the qualities of bodies — whether the same very ones or others are resumed. But since a question of this kind is held later, it will suffice meanwhile that from this too the resurrection is defined as bodily, when it is asked concerning the quality of bodies.

We have now come to flesh and blood, the very heart, in truth, of the whole question — which substances, with what condition the apostle disinherited from the kingdom of God, it is likewise to be learned from the preceding. "The first man," he says, "of the earth, earthy" — that is, of slime, that is, Adam; "the second man, from heaven" — that is, the word of God, that is, Christ; yet not otherwise man, though from heaven, except that He too is flesh and soul, which is man, which is Adam. For above too, called the last Adam, He drew the dealing of the name from the partnership of substance — since neither was Adam flesh from seed, which Christ also was not. "As, therefore, the earthy, such too the earthy; as the heavenly, such too the heavenly." Such in substance? or first in discipline, then in dignity too, which discipline grasped at? But by substance the earthy and the heavenly, once called by the apostle "men," will in no way be separated. For if Christ alone is truly heavenly — nay, even super-heavenly — yet man, in that He is flesh and soul, by nothing of that condition of substances is He discerned from the earthy quality; accordingly those too who are heavenly according to Him are understood proclaimed heavenly not of present substance, but of future brightness — because before, too, whence this distinction flowed, from the difference of dignity there was shown one glory of the super-heavenly, another of the super-earthly, and one of the sun, another of the moon, another of the stars, since star too differs from star in glory, yet not in substance. In short, having premised the difference of dignity in the same substance — to be followed now and to be grasped then — he subjoins also an exhortation: that here we follow the habit of Christ out of discipline, and there attain the height out of glory: "As we have borne the image of the earthy, let us bear too the image of the super-heavenly." For we have borne the image of the earthy through the college of transgression, through the partnership of death, through the exile of paradise. For although here the image of Adam is borne in the flesh, yet we are not admonished to lay aside the flesh; if not the flesh, then the conversation — that we may accordingly bear the image of the heavenly too in us, set now not as God, nor now in heaven, but walking according to the lineaments of Christ in sanctity and righteousness and truth. And so to discipline he directs this whole thing, so that here he says the image of Christ is to be borne in this flesh and in this time of discipline. For saying "let us bear" in the preceptive mode he speaks to this time, in which man is no other substance than flesh and soul; or, if any other — that is, heavenly — substance this faith regards, yet it is promised to that one to whom it is commanded to labour toward the other. Since, therefore, he constitutes the image both of the earthy and of the heavenly in the conversation — the one to be abjured, the other to be followed — then adds, "For this I say" (that is, on account of those things which I said above, for the conjunction is the supplement of the sense, rendering the antecedents), "that flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God by inheritance" — he commands flesh and blood to be understood as nothing else than the above-said image of the earthy; which, if it is reckoned in the conversation of oldness, but the conversation of oldness does not grasp the kingdom of God, accordingly flesh and blood, by not grasping the kingdom of God, are reduced to the conversation of oldness. Plainly, if the apostle never set substance for works, neither let him so use it here. But if those still set in the flesh he denied to be in the flesh — denying them to be in the works of the flesh — you ought to subvert its form, not its substance, but the works of the substance alienating from the kingdom of God. Which things being made manifest to the Galatians too, he professes that he foretells and has foretold that those who do such things shall not attain the kingdom of God by inheritance — not bearing, namely, the image of the heavenly, as they had borne the earthy, and therefore from their old conversation to be reckoned nothing else than flesh and blood. For even if the apostle had burst suddenly into this definition — that flesh and blood are to be eliminated from the kingdom of God — without any foundation-laying of a higher sense, should we not accordingly interpret those two substances as the old man given over to flesh and blood — that is, to eating and drinking — whose it is to say, against faith in the resurrection, "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die"? For this too the apostle, infulcing, has rebuked flesh and blood by their own fruits of eating and drinking.

But even setting aside interpretations of this kind, which charge the works of flesh and blood, it will be lawful to claim for resurrection the very substances themselves too, understood as nothing else than they are. For resurrection is not directly denied to flesh and blood, but the kingdom of God, which befalls resurrection (for there is also a resurrection unto judgment); nay rather, the general resurrection of the flesh is confirmed, when a special one is excepted. For while it is decreed into what state it does not rise, into what state it does rise is understood. And so, while according to merits the distinction of resurrection is suffered by the work of the substance, not the kind, it appears hence too that flesh and blood are kept from the kingdom of God under the name of fault, not of substance — yet under the name of their form they rise unto judgment, because they do not rise unto the kingdom. Still I will say: flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God by inheritance — rightly, alone and by themselves, that he might show the spirit still necessary to it. For it is the spirit that quickens unto the kingdom of God; the flesh profits nothing. Yet something else can profit it — that is, the spirit, and through the spirit the works of the spirit too. And so all flesh and blood rise equally in their own quality. But whose it is to enter the kingdom of God shall have to put on the power of incorruptibility and immortality, without which they cannot enter the kingdom of God before they can attain it. Rightly, then, flesh and blood, as we said, alone fail to grasp the kingdom of God. But now, since this corruptive — that is, the flesh — is to be devoured by incorruptibility, and this mortal — that is, the blood — by immortality, after the resurrection, out of transmutation, rightly flesh and blood, transmuted and devoured, can possess the kingdom of God by inheritance — yet not unless raised up. There are those who would have flesh and blood taken as Judaism, on account of circumcision — itself too foreign to the kingdom of God, because that too is reckoned to oldness, and is even elsewhere noted by the apostle under this title, who, after the Son of God was revealed in him to evangelize Him among the nations, did not at once refer it to flesh and blood — that is, to circumcision, that is, to Judaism — as he writes to the Galatians.

But it will now stand for all — even for the apostle himself, to be acquitted in truth of the greatest inconsiderateness — what we have reserved for the close: if so abruptly, as some would have it, with closed eyes, as they say, without distinction, without condition, he thrust out all flesh and blood everywhere from the kingdom of God — surely from the very royal palace of the heavens too, since there even now Jesus sits at the right hand of the Father, man, though God, the last Adam, though the primary word, flesh and blood, though purer than ours, yet the same in substance and in form in which He ascended, such also to descend, as the angels affirm — to be recognized, namely, by those who pierced Him through. He, called the sequester of God and of men, out of the deposit of either party committed to Him keeps in Himself the deposit of the flesh too, the earnest of the whole sum. For as He left us the earnest of the spirit, so too He received from us the earnest of the flesh, and bore it into heaven, the pledge of the whole sum to be one day brought together thither. Be secure, flesh and blood: you have usurped both heaven and the kingdom of God in Christ. Or, if they deny that you are in Christ, let them deny too that Christ is in heaven — they who have denied heaven to you. "So neither," he says, "shall corruption have incorruption by inheritance." Not that you should reckon flesh and blood to be corruption, when they are rather themselves liable to corruption — through death, namely; since it is death that not only corrupts but even consumes flesh and blood. But because he had decreed that the works of flesh and blood cannot attain the kingdom of God, the more to exaggerate this, he took away the inheritance of incorruption from corruption itself too — that is, from death, to which the works of flesh and blood are profitable. For a little after he expressed in a manner the death even of death itself: "Death is devoured," he says, "into contention. Where, O death, is your sting? where, O death, is your power?" But the sting of death is delinquency; this will be the corruption. But the power of delinquency is the law — that other one, without doubt, which he constituted in his members warring against the law of his mind, that very force of delinquency, namely, against the will. For above too he says that the last enemy, death, is made void. In this way too corruption shall not attain the inheritance of incorruption — that is, neither shall death endure. When and how is it to fail? When in an atom, in a momentary motion of the eye, at the last trumpet, the dead too shall rise incorrupt. Who these, if not those before corrupt — that is, bodies, that is, flesh and blood? "And we shall be transmuted." From what condition, if not that in which we shall be caught? "For this corruptive must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality." What mortal, if not the flesh? what corruptive, if not the blood? And lest you think the apostle to mean otherwise — providing for you, and labouring that you understand it said of the flesh, when he says "this corruptive" and "this mortal" — he says it holding the very skin. Surely he could not have pronounced "this" except of a subject, except of something present. It is a word of bodily demonstration. But one thing is "corruptive," another "corruption," and one thing "mortal," another "mortality." For one thing is that which suffers, another that which makes to suffer. So those things which suffer corruption and mortality, that is, flesh and blood, must of necessity suffer also incorruption and immortality.

Let us now see with what body he disputes the dead are to come. And it is well that he burst out at once to show, as though someone should ask of this kind. "Fool," he says, "what you sow is not made alive unless it has died." This, then, let it now be established from the example of the seed, that no other flesh is made alive than that very one which shall have died; and so the following things will shine forth. For nothing may be understood against the rule of the example; lest, because it follows, "And what you sow, you sow not the body that shall be," you therefore think another body shall rise than that which by dying is sown. For the rest, you have fallen away from the example. For never, wheat being sown and dissolved in the earth, does barley burst forth, and not that very kind of grain and the same nature and quality and form. In short, whence, if not that very thing? for corruption too is that very thing, since it is its own. For does he not also suggest how the body that shall be is not sown — saying, "But a bare grain, perchance, of wheat, or of some such thing; but God gives it a body as He wills"? Surely to that grain which he says is sown bare. Surely, you say. Then it is safe, to which God has to give a body. But how is it safe, if it is nowhere, if it does not rise, if that very thing does not rise? If it does not rise, it is not safe. If it is not safe either, it cannot receive a body from God. But indeed it is established in every way to be safe. To what end, then, shall God give it a body as He wills — it having surely its own body, that bare one — except that it may rise now not bare? Therefore that will be added which is built over the body, nor is that destroyed over which it is built, but increased. But that is safe which is increased. For the grain only is sown, without the vesture of a husk, without the foundation of an ear, without the defence of a beard, without the pride of a stalk. But it rises increased with abundance, built up with structure, framed in order, defended with adornment, and clothed throughout. These are to it a body from God, "another" — into which it is changed not by abolition, but by enlargement. "And to each of the seeds He has reckoned its own body" — not its own, that is, not its former — so that then that too be its own which it acquires from God from without. Keep, then, to the example, and preserve its mirror for the flesh, believing the same to bear fruit which is sown, the same, even if fuller, not another, even if returning otherwise. For it too shall receive the augmentation and adornment which God shall have willed to add to it according to merits. Without doubt to this he directs, "Not all flesh is the same flesh" — not to deny the communion of substance, but to make even the prerogative — reducing to a difference a body of honour, not of kind. To this end he subjoins also figured examples of animals and of elements. "One flesh of man" — that is, of the servant of God, who truly is man; "another of cattle" — that is, of the heathen (of whom the prophet too: "Man has been likened," he says, "to the irrational cattle"); "another flesh of birds" — that is, of the martyrs, who strive toward higher things; "another of fishes" — that is, of those for whom the water of baptism suffices. So too of the super-celestial bodies he commits his arguments. "One glory of the sun" — that is, of Christ; "and another of the moon" — that is, of the church; "and another of the stars" — that is, of the seed of Abraham. "For star differs from star in glory" — and "earthly and heavenly bodies," the Jew, namely, and the Christian. For the rest, if not figuratively, vainly enough did he set the flesh of mules and kites and the bodies of the heavenly luminaries beside human ones — they not pertaining to a comparison of condition, just as not to the consequence of resurrection. Finally, when through these he had concluded a difference of glory, not of substance, "So," he says, "is the resurrection of the dead too." How? Differing not in any other thing, but in glory alone. For again, recalling the resurrection to the same substance, and looking once more to the grain, "It is sown," he says, "in corruption, it rises in incorruption; it is sown in dishonour, it rises in glory; it is sown in weakness, it rises in power; it is sown a natural body, it rises a spiritual." Certainly nothing else rises than what is sown, nor is anything else sown than what is dissolved in the ground, nor is anything else dissolved in the ground than the flesh. For this the sentence of God dashed down: "Earth you are, and into earth you shall go" — because it too had been taken from the earth. Hence too the apostle conceived to say that it is sown, when it is rendered back into the earth, because for seeds too the earth is a place of safekeeping, to be there laid down and thence sought back. And therefore he reseals it, impressing, "For so it is written" — lest you think it anything else to be sown than "Into earth you shall go, from which you were taken"; so lest of any other than the flesh; for so it is written.

But "a natural body" some argue to be the soul, that they may call it away from the return of the flesh. Further, since it is established and fixed that the body shall rise which was sown, they will be challenged to the exhibition of the thing itself.
