Either let them show the soul sown after death — that is, dead, that is, dashed to the ground, scattered, dissolved (which is decreed upon it by God not at all) — let them set forth its corruption and dishonour, its weakness, that it too may rise unto incorruption and unto glory and unto power. But indeed in Lazarus, the chief example of resurrection, the flesh lay in weakness, the flesh had almost rotted into dishonour, the flesh meanwhile stank into corruption, and yet Lazarus rose as flesh — with the soul indeed, but the incorrupt one, which no one had bound with linen bands, no one had laid in a sepulchre, no one had now perceived to stink, no one had seen for four days sown. The whole condition, the whole issue of Lazarus the flesh of all men too experiences today, but the soul of none. In what, then, the pen of the apostle is found — concerning which it is established that he speaks — that will be both a natural body, when it is sown, and a spiritual, when it is raised up. For that you may so understand, he stretches out his hand still further, likewise weaving anew from the authority of the same Scripture the making of the first man Adam into a living soul. If Adam was the first man, but the flesh was man before the soul, without doubt the flesh shall have been made into a living soul. Further, when, being into a soul, it was a body, surely it was made a natural body. What would they have it called but that it was made through a soul, but that before the soul it was not, but that after the soul it shall not be — except when it rises? For, the soul received again, it is again made a natural body, that it may become a spiritual. For nothing rises except what was. So, whence it fits the flesh to be called a natural body, thence it in no way fits the soul. For the flesh is a body before it is a natural body. For having been animated afterward, it was made a natural body. But the soul, although a body — yet because it is itself a body not animated, but rather animating — cannot be called a natural body, nor become what it makes. For it makes the natural to be accidental to another; but, itself not accidental to another, how shall it make itself natural? As, therefore, before the natural body the flesh received the soul, so afterward, putting on the spiritual, it receives the spirit. This order the apostle, disposing it in Adam too and in Christ, rightly distinguishes, as in the heads of the distinction itself. And when he calls Christ the last Adam, recognize hence that He laboured with all the powers of His doctrine unto the resurrection of the flesh, not of the soul. For if the first man Adam too was flesh, not soul — who was at last made into a living soul — and the last Adam, Christ, is therefore Adam because man, therefore man because flesh, not because soul — and so he subjoins, "Not first that which is spiritual, but that which is natural, afterward that which is spiritual," according to either Adam. Does it seem to you that he distinguishes the natural body and the spiritual body in the same flesh, whose distinction in either Adam — that is, in either man — he laid the foundation of? For of what substance do Christ and Adam bring forth between themselves? Of the flesh, namely — though also of the soul. But under the name of flesh both are man; for first the flesh is man. From it too they could admit an order, that one be reckoned the first, the other the last man — that is, Adam. For the rest, diverse things cannot be disposed into an order, at least of substance. For of place or time or condition perhaps they can. But here, of the substance of the flesh, they are called the first and the last, as again "the first man of the earth, and the second from heaven"; because, even if from heaven according to the spirit, yet man according to the flesh. And so, since the order in either Adam fits the flesh, not the soul — that the first man be distinguished into a living soul, the last into a quickening spirit — equally their distinction prejudged a distinction of the flesh; so that it was said of the flesh, "Not first that which is spiritual, but that which is natural, afterward that which is spiritual," and so the same is to be understood above too: "And what is sown a natural body, and what rises a spiritual body," because "not first that which is spiritual, but that which is natural," because the first Adam into a soul, the last Adam into a spirit. The whole is of man, the whole of the flesh, since of man. What, then, shall we say? Has not the flesh even now the spirit from faith? — so that it must be asked how it is said to be sown a natural body. Plainly here too the flesh has received the spirit, but the earnest; the soul, however, not the earnest, but the fullness. And so for this reason too, under the name of the greater substance, it was named a natural body, in which it is sown, being accordingly through the fullness of the spirit moreover spiritual, in which it is raised up. What wonder, if it is named rather from that with which it is filled than from that with which it is sprinkled?

So very many questions are suborned from the occasions of words, as also from the communities of words. For because that too is set down in the apostle, "That the mortal be devoured by life" — the flesh, namely — they snatch even "devouring" unto the perdition of the flesh — as though we are not said to "devour" gall and grief, that is, to hide and cover and contain them within ourselves. In short, since that too is written, "This mortal must put on immortality," it is shown how the mortal is devoured by life — while, clothed with immortality, it is hidden and covered and contained within, not while it is consumed and lost. "Then death too," you say, "shall be safe, when it has been devoured." Therefore discern, according to the senses, the community of words, and you understand wholly. For one thing is death, another the mortal. So in one way death shall be devoured, in another the mortal. Death does not grasp immortality, but the mortal does. In short, it is even written that this mortal must put on immortality. How, then, does it grasp it, while devoured by life? How is it devoured by life, while received and reduced and included into it? For the rest, death is rightly devoured into destruction, because it too devours unto this. "Death," he says, "devoured by prevailing, and therefore is devoured into contention. Where, O death, is your sting? where, O death, is your contention?" Accordingly life too — death's rival, namely — through contention shall devour unto salvation what through its own contention death had devoured unto destruction.

Although, therefore, by proving that the flesh shall rise we prove by this very thing that no other shall rise than that which is in question, yet the several questions and their causes demand their own encounters too, though already cut down from another side. We will interpret, then, more fully both the force and the reason of transmutation, which commonly ministers the presumption of another flesh about to rise — as though to be transmuted is to cease to be wholly and to perish from the former. But transmutation must be distinguished from every argument of perdition. For one thing is transmutation, another perdition. Further, it is not another, if the flesh shall be so transmuted as to perish. But it shall perish, transmuted, if it shall not itself remain in the transmutation which shall have been exhibited in the resurrection. For as it perishes if it does not rise, so too if it indeed rises, but is withdrawn into a transmutation, it equally perishes. For it shall equally not be, as if it had not risen. And how foolish, if it rise to this end, that it be not — which could not have risen, and not be, because it had now begun not to be! Things diverse shall in no way be mingled, change and perdition — in their works diverse. The one perishes, the other changes. As, therefore, what is perished is not changed, so what is changed is not perished. For to have perished is wholly not to be what one was; to have been changed is to be otherwise. Further, while it is otherwise, it can be that very thing; for it has being, which does not perish. For it has suffered change, not perdition. And so a thing can both be transmuted and none the less be itself — as the whole man too in this age is indeed himself in substance, yet is in many ways transmuted — in habit and in very corpulence and in health and in condition and in dignity and in age, in pursuit, in business, in craft, in resources, in seats, in laws, in manners — and yet loses nothing of the man, nor is so made another that he ceases to be the same; nay, is not made another, but other. This form of transmutation the divine documents too attest. The hand of Moses is changed, and indeed after the likeness of a dead one — bloodless and whitened, cold; but, heat recovered and colour poured back, it is the same flesh and blood. His face too is afterward changed with a brightness not to be gazed on. But Moses was likewise he who was not seen. So too Stephen had now put on the angelic height, but no other knees sank under the stoning. The Lord too, in the recess of the mountain, had changed even His garments with light, but had kept His lineaments recognizable to Peter; where also Moses and Elijah — the one in the image of flesh not yet recovered, the other in the truth of flesh not yet deceased — yet taught that the same condition of the body endures even in glory. Instructed by which example Paul too says, "Who transfigured the body of our humility, conformable to the body of His glory." But if you defend both transfiguration and conversion as a passing-over of each one's substance, then Saul too, converted into another man, departed from his own body, and Satan himself, when he is transfigured into an angel of light, loses his own quality. I think not. So too in the event of the resurrection it will be lawful to be changed, converted, reformed, with the safety of the substance.

For how absurd, how unjust indeed — but both how unworthy of God — that one substance should labour, another be discharged with the wage; that this flesh should be torn by martyrdoms, but another be crowned; likewise, on the contrary, that this flesh should wallow in filth, but another be condemned! Is it not better at once to lead away all faith from the hope of resurrection than to make sport of the gravity and justice of God? Marcion to be raised up for Valentinus? — since it is not credible that the mind or the memory or the conscience of the present-day man should be abolished through that exchanging garment of immortality and incorruption — the emolument and fruit of resurrection being thus idle, and the state of the divine judgment on either side. If I shall not remember that I am he who deserved, how shall I give glory to God? how shall I sing Him a new song, not knowing that I am he who owes the grace? But why is the transmutation of the flesh alone excepted, and not of the soul too at the same time, which in all things presided over the flesh? How is it that the same soul which in this flesh ran through the whole order of life, which in this flesh learned God and put on Christ and sowed the hope of salvation, should in some other flesh I know not which reap the fruit? Truly that flesh is most gracious, for which life shall stand free of charge. But if the soul too shall not be changed, then there is no resurrection of the soul either; for not even it shall be believed to have risen, if it has not risen another.

Hence now comes that subtlety of vulgar incredulity. "If," they say, "the very same substance is recalled with its own form, line, quality, then with its remaining marks too. And so the blind and the lame and the paralytic, and as anyone has departed marked, so too he shall return." What now, even if you so disdain to attain so great a grace, of whatever kind, from God? For do you not even now, admitting the salvation of the soul alone, ascribe the same to halved men? What is it to believe the resurrection, except to believe it entire? For if the flesh shall be repaired from dissolution, much more shall it be recalled from vexation. By lesser things they prejudge the greater. Is not the truncation or blunting of any member a death of the member? If universal death is rescinded by resurrection, what of the partial? If we are transmuted into glory, how much more into soundness? The maiming of bodies is an accidental thing; integrity is proper. In this we are born. Even if we are vexed in the womb, it is now a passion of the man. The kind is before the mischance. As life is conferred by God, so too it is restored. As we receive it, such too we recover it. We are rendered back to nature, not to injury; we revive as we are born, not as we are harmed. If God does not raise up the whole, He does not raise up the dead. For what dead man is whole, even if he dies whole? Who is sound who is breathless? What body is unharmed, when slain, when cold, when grown pale, when stiff, when a corpse? When is a man more disabled than when he is wholly so? When more paralytic than when immovable? So to be raised up a dead man is nothing else than to be made whole, lest in that part he be still dead in which he has not risen. God is fit to remake what He made. This His power and bounty He has now sufficiently pledged in Christ — nay, even shown — not only the raiser of the flesh, but also its reintegrator. And so the apostle too: "And the dead," he says, "shall rise incorrupt." How, if not whole — they who before were corrupt as much by the vice of health as by the senility of burial? For above too, proposing both — that this corruptive must put on incorruption, and this mortal immortality — he did not repeat the sentence, but charged a difference. For dividing immortality unto the rescinding of death, incorruption unto the obliteration of corruption, he tempered the one to the resurrection, the other to the reintegration. I think, moreover, that to the Thessalonians too he promised the integrity of the whole substance. And so neither henceforth shall the ruins of bodies be feared. Integrity, whether preserved or restored, will be able to lose nothing — since to it even what it had lost, if it had lost anything, is given back. For prescribing still that the flesh shall undergo the same sufferings, if it be said to rise the same, you rashly defend nature against her Lord, you impiously assert law against grace — as though it were not lawful for the Lord God both to change nature and to preserve it without law. How, then, do we read, "The things impossible with men are possible with God," and, "God has chosen the foolish things of the world, that He may confound the wisdom of the world"? I ask you — if you should change your slave by liberty, since the same flesh and soul shall remain which before had been liable to scourges and fetters and brands, ought he therefore to suffer those same things? I think not. Rather he is honoured with the brightness of a white robe and the honour of a golden ring and the name and tribe and table of a patron. Permit this power to God too — by the force of transmutation to reform that one's condition, not its nature — while both the sufferings are taken away and defences are conferred. So the flesh shall indeed remain even after the resurrection, so far passible as it is itself, as it is the same — yet so far impassible as it is for this very thing manumitted by the Lord, that it may no longer be able to suffer.

"Eternal gladness," says Isaiah, "upon their head." Nothing eternal, except after the resurrection. "Pain and mourning and groaning," he says, "shall flee from them." Accordingly too the angel to John: "And God shall wipe away every tear from their eyes" — surely from those same eyes which had before wept, and which could still weep, did not the divine indulgence dry up every shower of tears. And again: "For God shall wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death thus far" — therefore corruption thus far too; accordingly driven away by incorruption, just as death by immortality. If pain and mourning and groaning and death itself come from the injuries of both soul and flesh, how shall they be taken away, unless the causes have ceased — namely the injuries of flesh and soul? Where are adverse mischances with God? or where the hostile assaults with Christ? where the demonic onsets with the Holy Spirit — the devil himself with his angels now plunged into the fires? where necessity, or what is called fortune or fate? what blow to the raised-up after pardon? what wrath to the reconciled after grace? what weakness after power? what infirmity after salvation? That the garments and sandals of the sons of Israel remained for those forty years unworn and unwasted; that even in the bodies themselves justice fixed the easy growths of nails and hairs to a fitness of habit and dignity, lest even an enormity of corruption be reckoned; that the Babylonian fires injured neither the tiaras nor the trousers of the three brothers, though foreign to Jews; that Jonah, devoured by the beast of the sea, in whose belly shipwrecks were being digested, after three days is spat out unharmed; that today Enoch and Elijah — not yet discharged by resurrection, because not yet having undergone death, yet translated from the world, and these very ones now candidates of eternity — learn an immunity of the flesh from every vice and from every loss and from every injury and contumely: to what faith do they set a seal of testimony, except that by which it ought to be believed that these are documents of future integrity? "For these were figures of us," the apostle being author, "which were written" — that we may both believe the Lord more powerful than every law of bodies, and surely the more the preserver of the flesh, whose very garments, very sandals, He protected.

"But the future age," you say, "is of another disposition and an eternal one; therefore the substance of this age, not eternal, cannot possess a different one." Plainly, if man is on account of the future disposition, and not the disposition on account of man. But indeed the apostle, writing, "Whether the world, or life, or death, or things future, or things present, all are yours," has constituted the same men heirs even of things future. Isaiah grants you nothing, saying, "All flesh is grass," and elsewhere, "And all flesh shall see the salvation of God." He distinguished issues, not substances. For who has not set the judgment of God in a double sentence of salvation and penalty? "All flesh," therefore, "is grass" — that which is appointed to fire; and "all flesh shall see the salvation of God" — that which is ordained to salvation. I know of myself that I have neither committed adulteries with another flesh, nor now strive toward continence with another flesh. If anyone is carrying about double privy parts, he can now both take away the grass of the unclean flesh and reserve for himself alone that which shall see the salvation of God. But since the same prophet also shows the nations now reckoned as it were dust and spittle, now about to hope and believe in the name and in the arm of the Lord — are we deceived about the nations too? and are some indeed about to believe, others reckoned into dust, out of a diversity of substance? But even Christ, beyond the ocean, and from this heaven which lies upon us, shone forth the true light to the nations. And the Valentinians themselves have learned to err here; nor will the form of the believing nations be other than that of the unbelieving too — of flesh, of soul. As, therefore, He distinguished the same nations not by kind, but by lot, so too the fleshes — which in those very nations are one substance — He disjoined not by material, but by wage.

But behold — that they may still exaggerate the controversy against the flesh, against that very same flesh most of all — he argues also from the offices of the members; either saying that they too ought to remain in their works and fruits, as ascribed to the same corpulence, or, because it is agreed that the offices of the members are to depart, that they may scrape away the corpulence too, whose perseverance, namely, is not to be believed, as being without members, because members are not to be believed without offices either. "For to what end now," they say, "this cavern of the mouth and station of the teeth and slope of the throat and crossways of the stomach and gulf of the belly and the tangled length of the intestines, when there shall be no place for eating and drinking? to what end do members of this kind admit, subdue, roll down, divide, digest, expel? to what end the hands themselves and feet and all the labouring limbs, when even the care of food shall cease? to what end the kidneys, conscious of seeds, and the rest of the genitals of either sex, and the stables of conceptions, and the founts of the breasts, when coition and offspring and rearing shall depart? finally, to what end the whole body, the whole, namely, about to be idle?" To these things, then, we have laid the foundation that the dispositions of things future and present ought not to be confused, transmutation being about to intervene then; and now we build on that these offices of the members hold together for the necessities of this life so long until that very life too be transferred from temporality into eternity, as the natural body into the spiritual, while this mortal puts on immortality and this corruptive incorruption; and that very life freed then from necessities, the members too shall be freed from offices — yet not on that account shall they not be. For although they be freed from offices, yet they are retained for tokens, that each may carry back through the body according as he has done. For the tribunal of God demands man safe; but safe he cannot be without members, of whose not offices, but substances, he consists. Unless perhaps you will assert a ship safe without a keel, without a prow, without a stern, without the soundness of the whole frame. And yet a ship scattered by a storm or dissolved by rot, all its members brought back and recured, we have often beheld the same, glorying even in the title of restoration. Are we tormented over the workmanship and judgment and right of God? Further, if a rich and bountiful master, indulging his own affection or glory, willed the restoration of the ship only to work this far, will you therefore deny the former frame necessary to it, as though henceforth idle, since restoration alone, without operation, befits the safety of the ship? Therefore it suffices to learn only this: whether the Lord, in appointing man to salvation, has appointed the flesh; whether He wishes the same to be anew, which you may not, from the future idleness of the members, prescribe to be unable to be anew. For a thing may be anew and none the less be idle; but it cannot be said to be idle if it is not. But indeed if it is, it can also not be idle; for nothing with God shall be idle.

But you have received, O man, a mouth for devouring and drinking: why not rather for speaking, that you may differ from the other animals? why not rather for preaching God, that you may even preside over men? In short, Adam named the animals before he plucked from the tree, prophesied even before he devoured. But you have received teeth for gnawing meat: why not rather for crowning your every gape and opening? why not rather for tempering the beats of the tongue, for marking with their stop the articulations of the voice? In short, hear that there are even toothless men, and see how you require the instrument of teeth too for the honour of the mouth. Lower openings are bored in man and in woman, surely by which lusts may flow: why are they not rather cultivated as about to flow off? There is still in women within a place where seeds may be gathered; or is it where the burdens of blood may withdraw, which the more sluggish sex does not suffice to shake off? For these things too must be said, since they bark in mockery, of set purpose to flood out the resurrection — what offices of members they wish, and how they wish, and of whom they wish — not reconsidering that the very causes of necessity shall then be idle: of food, hunger; and of drink, thirst; and of coition, generation; and of operation, livelihood. For death taken away, neither the props of food shall be a burden to the members, as defences of life, nor the equipment of generation. For the rest, even today it is lawful to be idle of intestines and privy parts. For forty days Moses and Elijah, discharging a fast, were fed by God alone. For even then it was being dedicated, "Man lives not on bread, but on the word of God." Behold the lineaments of future virtue. We too, as we can, excuse the mouth from food, even withdraw the sex from intercourse. How many voluntary eunuchs? how many virgins married to Christ? how many barren of either nature, built with unfruitful genitals? For if even here it is now to be idle, both of the offices and of the emoluments of the members, by a temporal idleness, as in a temporal disposition, and yet man is no less safe — accordingly, man being safe, and indeed the more then, as in an eternal disposition, the more shall we not desire those things which we have already grown accustomed here not to desire.

But to this discussion the Lord's pronouncement sets an end. "They shall be," He says, "as the angels." If not by marrying, because not by dying — surely also by sinking under no like necessity of the bodily condition — since the angels too were sometime as men, eating and drinking and offering their feet to the washing; for they had put on a human surface, their own substance safe within. Therefore, if angels, made as men, took up in the same substance of spirit a carnal handling, why should not men too, made as angels, undergo in the same substance of flesh a spiritual disposition — no more liable to the solemnities of the flesh under an angelic garment than the angels then to the solemnities of the spirit under a human one? — nor therefore not about to remain in the flesh, because not in the solemnities of the flesh; since neither did the angels therefore not remain in the spirit, because not in the solemnities of the spirit. In short, He did not say, "They shall be angels," lest He deny them men, but, "as the angels," that He might preserve them men. He did not take away the substance to which He attributed the likeness.

The flesh, therefore, shall rise again — and indeed all of it, and indeed the very same, and indeed entire. It is on deposit, wheresoever, with God, through that most faithful sequester of God and men, Jesus Christ, who shall render both God to man and man to God, the spirit to the flesh and the flesh to the spirit. He has now confederated both in Himself; He has matched the bride to the bridegroom and the bridegroom to the bride. For even if anyone shall contend that the soul is the bride, yet even in the name of dowry the flesh shall follow the soul. The soul shall not be a prostitute, to be received naked by the bridegroom. It has its equipment, its adornment, its bond-servant, the flesh, which shall accompany it as a foster-sister. But the flesh is the bride, which also in Christ Jesus contracted the spirit for bridegroom through blood. The downfall of this, which you suppose, know to be a withdrawal. The soul is not set apart alone. The flesh too has its withdrawals meanwhile — in waters, in fires, in birds, in beasts; when it seems to be dissolved into these, it is, as it were, poured into vessels. If the vessels themselves too fail, when out of them too it has flowed into its mother earth, it is reabsorbed as it were by a roundabout way, that from her it may be presented anew — an Adam to hear from the Lord, "Behold, Adam is become as one of us" — then truly possessed of the evil which he escaped, and of the good which he gained. Why, O soul, do you envy the flesh? No one is so near to you, whom you should love after the Lord; no one is more your brother, who is born with you even in God. You ought rather to have entreated resurrection for it; through you, perhaps, it sinned. But it is no wonder if you have hated her whose author too you have spurned — whom you have grown accustomed either to deny or to change even in Christ — accordingly corrupting even the very word of God, who was made flesh, either by pen or by interpretation, drawing over besides the secrets of apocrypha, the fables of blasphemy. But indeed God almighty, against these inventions of incredulity and perversity, by His most provident grace pouring out in the last days from His spirit upon all flesh, upon His servants and handmaids, has both animated the labouring faith of the carnal resurrection and purged the former instruments of every obscurity of ambiguity by the manifest lights of words and senses. For because heresies had to be, that the approved might be made manifest, and these could not dare without some occasions of the Scriptures, therefore the former instruments seem to have ministered to them certain materials — yet themselves refutable by those same letters. But since it was not fitting that the Holy Spirit should dissemble, but that He should overflow even with words of this kind, which should scatter the seeds of no heretics' cunning — nay, should pluck up even their old turfs — therefore He has now dispelled all former ambiguities, and whatever parables they will, by an open and perspicuous preaching of the whole sacrament, overflowing through the new prophecy that streams down from the Paraclete. If you drink His founts, you will be able to thirst for no doctrine; no ardour of questions will consume you; by drinking on every side, you will cool also the resurrection of the flesh.
